title: The Middle Ages in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe the thousand years between Rome's fall in the West and the Renaissance.
summary: The Middle Ages run from the collapse of Roman rule in the West to the Renaissance, roughly 500 to 1500, and split into early, high and late periods.

cards.headline: The Middle Ages lasted about a thousand years. That’s a lot for one name.
cards.body: Before the castles and the crusades, start with the frame: when the Middle Ages were, and how historians slice them.

cards.headline: From Rome to the Renaissance
cards.body: The Middle Ages is the period of European history from the collapse of Roman rule in the West, in the 5th century, to the Renaissance. In round numbers: about 500 to about 1500. The usual starting marker is 476, when the last emperor in the West lost his throne. The finish line is blurrier, because the Renaissance arrived in different parts of Europe at different times. Think of it like a sunrise: easy to see it has happened, hard to name the exact minute.
cards.callout: About 500 to about 1500: roughly a thousand years

events.label: The early Middle Ages begin

mascot.line: A thousand years under one name. Imagine one label for everything from the 1020s to today!

cards.headline: Why slice it at all?
cards.body: Because a thousand years is far too long to be one thing. Someone living in 500 and someone living in 1500 were as far apart in time as you are from the 1020s. The early period, about 500 to 1000, was a time of frequent warfare, when town life in western Europe virtually disappeared. The centuries that followed looked very different. So historians split the age into early, high and late, the way you might split your own life into childhood, school and work.

title: Why "Middle" Ages?
objective: After this level you can explain where the name came from and why historians question the idea of "Dark Ages".
summary: Renaissance scholars named the Middle Ages as a dark gap between antiquity and their own revival. Historians now rarely say "Dark Ages" because of the judgment it carries.

cards.headline: Nobody in the Middle Ages thought they lived in the middle of anything.
cards.body: The name was stuck on later, by people who saw the whole thousand years as a gap to hurry past. Who named it, and why do historians push back?

cards.headline: In the middle of what?
cards.body: Italian scholars of the Renaissance invented the idea. They admired ancient Greece and Rome and saw their own age as a revival of classical learning. Everything in between became a middle period: a thousand years of darkness and ignorance, in their telling. Our word medieval still carries the idea. It comes from Latin medium, “the middle”, and aevum, “age”. Picture a sandwich where the people who named it only cared about the bread.

cards.headline: Petrarch turns out the lights
cards.body: One of the first to paint it dark was the Italian scholar Petrarch, in the 14th century. He wrote of living in a dark time that had begun with the decline of the Roman Empire. For Petrarch, ancient Rome was the light, and the centuries since were the shadow it left behind. It was a powerful image, and a stubborn one.
cards.callout: Ancient Rome = light; everything after = dark, in Petrarch’s picture

mascot.line: Rule of thumb: when a whole era gets called “dark”, check who was holding the lamp.

cards.headline: Why historians dropped “Dark Ages”
cards.body: Historians now rarely use the term “Dark Ages” because of the value judgment it carries. Some defend it as meaning only that we have few written records from the period, but its usual sense is a time of ignorance and barbarity. And the evidence keeps turning on lights. In Level 9 you’ll dig up a ship burial that reshaped how historians see early England, showing a society far more sophisticated than “dark” suggests.

title: After Rome Fell
objective: After this level you can describe the kingdoms that replaced the Western Roman Empire.
summary: In 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor but ruled as king. Germanic kingdoms (Ostrogoths, Visigoths, Vandals, Franks, Anglo-Saxons) took over, often keeping Roman ways.

cards.headline: Rome’s western empire ended in 476. Its new ruler still bowed to an emperor.
cards.body: A Roman one, in Constantinople. Not much of a revolution. So what actually changed when Rome fell in the West, and who took over?

cards.headline: 476: a convenient line
cards.body: In 476 the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor in the West. Then he didn’t crown himself emperor. He called himself king, and he recognized the eastern emperor, Zeno, as his overlord. That’s why 476 is traditionally the end of the Western Empire: it’s a tidy line drawn across a messy change. Nobody in Italy woke up the next morning and said, “Ah, the Middle Ages.” That name came centuries later.

items.label: In the north

cards.headline: Theodoric: a Goth running Rome’s paperwork
cards.body: In 489 the Ostrogoth king Theodoric invaded Italy. In 493 he killed Odoacer, and he ruled Italy until 526. Yet the old Roman civil service carried on more or less unchanged. Only Goths served in the army; Romans ran the government. Theodoric and his Goths were Arian Christians, not Catholics, like the Visigoths in Spain. New king, new army, same paperwork: that’s what the fall of Rome often looked like on the ground.

title: The Byzantine Empire
objective: After this level you can explain how the Eastern Roman Empire lasted another thousand years.
summary: The eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453. Its Greek-speaking people called themselves Romans; layered walls and a trusted gold coin helped it endure.

cards.headline: Rome didn’t end in 476. Half of it kept going for about another thousand years.
cards.body: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, outlasted the West by almost a millennium, until 1453. How does an empire lose half of itself and carry on?

cards.headline: Romans, not Byzantines
cards.body: Historians call it the Byzantine Empire, after Byzantium, the old Greek town where Constantinople was founded in 330. Its people never called themselves Byzantines. They called themselves Romaioi: Romans. Over time, Greek replaced Latin as the language of government. So picture Roman emperors, running the Roman Empire, in Greek, and puzzled by the name we gave them.

mascot.line: Moat, wall, bigger wall. Constantinople did not believe in a welcome mat.

cards.headline: Three walls deep
cards.body: Constantinople’s best defense was its land walls, begun under Emperor Theodosius II in 412. An attacker faced a moat, then an outer wall, then a taller main wall studded with 96 towers. Those walls held firm through the early Middle Ages against Germanic, Hun, Avar, Slav and Arab attackers. The city fell only in 1453, to Ottoman forces armed with heavy cannon. Attackers had to win three times in a row; defenders only had to win once.

cards.fact: Its gold coin was trusted far beyond its borders.
cards.context: The solidus, which westerners called the bezant, weighed about 4.5 grams and was known for its purity for centuries. It dominated European trade until the 13th century. Think of it as the medieval world’s dollar: accepted far from the empire that minted it. Strong walls kept enemies out; good gold kept business coming in.

title: Justinian and Hagia Sophia
objective: After this level you can describe Justinian's law code and his great church.
summary: Justinian (527-565) had Roman law sorted into the Corpus Juris Civilis, the root of today's civil law, and built Hagia Sophia (532-537) with its floating dome.

cards.headline: In 532 a riot burned Constantinople’s great church. Justinian built a finer one.
cards.body: It was finished by 537. Same emperor, same busy decade: he also had Rome’s tangled laws sorted out. Two projects, one of law and one of stone, both built to last.

cards.headline: The great legal spring clean
cards.body: Roman law had piled up for hundreds of years, and the rules often contradicted each other. Justinian, emperor from 527 to 565, had it sorted. Between 530 and 533 a commission of 16 lawyers led by Tribonian boiled centuries of legal writing down into the Digest, in 50 books. Contradictions were removed, and any law left out was repealed. It was the ultimate clear-out: if it isn’t in the book, it isn’t the law.

cards.headline: Law that outlived the empire
cards.body: Justinian’s collections came to be known together as the Corpus Juris Civilis, the “Body of Civil Law”. Through them, Roman law became the foundation of civil law, the legal system used today across continental Europe and Latin America. Remember Level 4’s Romans who spoke Greek? Their emperor’s rulebook is still in court every day, from Paris to Buenos Aires.

cards.headline: A dome on a ring of light
cards.body: Hagia Sophia, “Holy Wisdom”, was designed by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus. Its main dome is about 32 meters across. Windows pierce its base, so in daylight the supports seem to vanish and the dome looks as if it floats. The historian Procopius wrote that it seemed “suspended from heaven by that golden chain”. Heavy stone, made to look weightless: that was the trick.

cards.fact: For nearly a thousand years, it was the largest cathedral in Christendom.
cards.context: Finished in 537, Hagia Sophia held that record for close to a millennium: roughly from Justinian’s day to the end of the Middle Ages.

title: The Franks
objective: After this level you can explain how Clovis and the Franks built a kingdom in Gaul.
summary: Clovis (481-511) united the Franks, took most of Gaul and made Paris his capital. His Catholic baptism won him the bishops and most of his subjects.

cards.headline: France takes its name from a Germanic people: the Franks.
cards.body: Its favorite royal name comes from one of their kings, Clovis, and a form of his name, Louis, became the most common name of French kings. The Franks went on to build the most powerful Christian kingdom in early medieval western Europe. It started with him.

cards.headline: Clovis takes Gaul
cards.body: Clovis became king of the Franks in 481. He forced the other Frankish groups to accept his rule, and in 486 he took over the last Roman-ruled territory in Gaul. In 507 he defeated the Visigoths and took Aquitaine, in southwestern Gaul. (Remember Level 3’s Visigoths ruling from Toledo? This is why their kingdom ended up in Spain.) Then he made Paris his capital.

mascot.line: Same church as the people you rule. Clovis made a smart move there.

cards.headline: The baptism that mattered
cards.body: The Goths had become Arian Christians, like Theodoric in Level 3. Clovis, whose wife Clotilda was a Catholic, was baptized a Catholic Christian at Reims by Bishop Remigius. The date is debated: sources give dates including 498 and 508. Either way, it put him on the same side as the church and the Catholic majority he ruled. That spared Gaul the long conflicts other Germanic kingdoms went through. Same faith as your subjects: a strong foundation for a kingdom.

cards.headline: Split four ways
cards.body: When Clovis died in 511, his kingdom was divided among his four surviving sons. Not the tidiest inheritance. Yet his family, the Merovingian dynasty, ruled for more than 200 years. The Franks’ story was far from over.

title: Monasteries
objective: After this level you can explain how monks copied books and kept learning alive.
summary: Benedict's Rule balanced prayer, work and reading. Monks copied books by hand in scriptoria, and Cassiodorus had his monks copy pagan classics too.

cards.headline: Scribes often said: “Two fingers hold the pen, but the whole body toils.”
cards.body: They knew. In the early Middle Ages, books found refuge in monasteries, and every one was copied by hand, letter by letter. So why were monks the ones holding the pens?

cards.headline: A rule for living
cards.body: In 529 Benedict of Nursia founded a monastery at Monte Cassino in Italy. He wrote a Rule for it that balanced prayer, work and study: about five hours of manual work and four of reading scripture and spiritual writings a day, with enough food and sleep. Moderate, as monastic life goes. By the early 9th century his Rule had replaced most others across northern and western Europe. One man’s timetable became a continent’s.

cards.headline: Why monks copied
cards.body: Benedict didn’t set out to build libraries. But monks needed service books, Bibles and the writings of the Church Fathers, and the only way to get a book was to copy one. So monasteries set aside a writing room, the scriptorium, where scribes copied manuscripts onto parchment or vellum, made from animal skin. No printer, no photocopier: just a pen and a very long afternoon.

cards.headline: Saving the pagans
cards.body: Cassiodorus, who had served as a senior official under Theodoric (Level 3’s Gothic king of Italy), founded a monastery called Vivarium around 540. He had its monks copy pagan as well as Christian authors, and other monasteries later followed his example. It mattered, because books were scarce: a monastic library of 600 volumes counted as fairly large. A small-town library today would have looked like a miracle.
cards.callout: Copy it, or lose it: every book existed only as many times as someone wrote it out

title: The Rise of Islam
objective: After this level you can describe how Islam began and spread in its first century.
summary: Muhammad (born about 570) preached in Mecca; Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to him by God. After 622 and his death in 632, caliphs built an empire from Spain to the Indus.

cards.headline: In 622 Muhammad moved to Medina. Muslims still count their years from it.
cards.body: That journey from Mecca began a new calendar. By the early 8th century, the empire of his successors stretched from Spain to the Indus River. Here’s how that began.

cards.headline: A prophet in Mecca
cards.body: Muhammad was born around 570 in Mecca, in Arabia. By tradition, in 610 he had a vision of the angel Gabriel. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the word of God, revealed to Muhammad in stages through Gabriel. In 622 he moved from Mecca to Medina. That move, the hijra, marks the start of the Islamic calendar. Your calendar counts from one starting point; this one counts from a journey.

cards.headline: The successors
cards.body: Muhammad died in Medina in 632. The leaders who followed were called caliphs, from khalifah, “successor”. Under the first four caliphs, Arab Muslim armies beat the Byzantines at Yarmuk in 636, took Syria and Egypt from them, and defeated the armies of Persia. Remember Level 4? Byzantium lost Syria and Egypt, but Constantinople’s walls held against Arab attackers.

cards.headline: From Spain to the Indus
cards.body: The Umayyad caliphs, from 661, moved the capital from Medina to Damascus. Under them, Muslim forces took North Africa and, from 711, overran most of Spain, ending the Visigothic kingdom you met in Level 3. By the early 8th century the caliphate reached from Spain to Central Asia and the Indus valley. Conquered Christians and Jews, whom Muslims called People of the Book, could keep their religion as long as they paid taxes.

title: Anglo-Saxon England
objective: After this level you can describe the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and the treasure of Sutton Hoo.
summary: Angles, Saxons and Jutes built kingdoms in Britain after Roman rule ended; England means "land of the Angles". The Sutton Hoo ship burial showed their wealth.

cards.headline: In 1939 a buried ship turned up in Suffolk. Its wood had long since vanished.
cards.body: Yet the ship was still there. Rows of iron rivets traced its ghost in the sand, some 27 metres long. Inside lay a treasure fit for a king. But first: whose England was this?

cards.headline: Land of the Angles
cards.body: Roman rule in Britain ended about 410. Germanic peoples, chiefly Angles, Saxons and Jutes, came to rule much of what is now England (archaeology suggests some had arrived even earlier). They built kingdoms, including Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia, Essex, Sussex, Wessex and Kent. The Angles gave the country its name: England comes from Old English Engla land, “land of the Angles”. The Anglo-Saxons ruled until the Norman Conquest of 1066.

mascot.line: The wood was gone, but the nails remembered exactly where it had been.

cards.headline: The ghost ship
cards.body: At Sutton Hoo, landowner Edith Pretty hired local archaeologist Basil Brown to dig the mounds on her land. In May 1939 he struck iron rivets. The ship’s wood had decayed, but the rivets and its outline in the sand showed a vessel some 27 metres long. No body was found; later chemical analysis suggested it had dissolved in the acidic soil. A ship made of nothing but its nails, and a grave with no one in it.

cards.headline: Treasure fit for a king
cards.body: The burial held 263 finds of gold, garnet, silver, bronze and more, including a famous helmet and objects from far-off Byzantium. It is usually thought to be the grave of Rædwald, a king of East Anglia who died around 624. Edith Pretty gave the whole treasure to the British Museum in 1939. And it changed minds: a period once dismissed as the “Dark Ages” turned out to be rich, skilled and connected to a wider world.

title: Charlemagne
objective: After this level you can explain how Charlemagne built an empire and revived learning.
summary: Charlemagne, king of the Franks from 768 to 814, conquered much of western Europe and revived learning: Alcuin, schools, copied classics and a clear new script.

cards.headline: The small letters on this screen go back to Charlemagne’s scribes.
cards.body: Yet the king behind them never quite learned to write. Charlemagne conquered much of western Europe, then set out to fill it with schools and books.

cards.headline: Charles the Great
cards.body: Charlemagne means Charles the Great, and he was king of the Franks from 768 until his death in 814. His family was new to the throne: in 751 his father, Pippin, had taken it from the last Merovingian king. (Remember Clovis’s dynasty from Level 6? This is where its run ended.) Charlemagne spent much of his reign at war. He became king of the Lombards, in Italy, in 774, and fought the Saxons for about 30 years until they submitted in 804. By the end, his realm covered much of western Europe.

cards.headline: A school in the palace
cards.body: Conquest was only half the plan. In 781 Charlemagne invited Alcuin of York, an English scholar, to head the palace school at Aachen. Monasteries and other church institutions added schools of their own. Remember Level 7’s monks copying books by hand? Now scholars copied large numbers of classical Latin texts, many of which might otherwise have been lost. Historians call this revival the Carolingian Renaissance.

mascot.line: Tablets under the pillow for late-night practice. Even emperors do homework in bed.

cards.headline: The king who couldn’t write
cards.body: The copyists used a new handwriting, Carolingian minuscule, clear and easy to read. Centuries later, Renaissance scholars revived it, and it became the basis of the roman type you’re reading right now. The irony? His biographer Einhard wrote that Charlemagne kept writing tablets under his pillow to practise his letters, but he started too late in life and never mastered it. The man behind Europe’s handwriting struggled with his own.

title: An Emperor in 800
objective: After this level you can explain why the Pope crowning Charlemagne emperor mattered.
summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor, the first in the West since Rome fell there. Byzantium called it usurpation; Verdun later split the empire.

cards.headline: On Christmas Day 800, Charlemagne went to church a king and left an emperor.
cards.body: No one in the West had held that title since Rome fell there. So who gave it to him, and why did it matter so much?

cards.headline: A pope on the run
cards.body: The story starts with a pope in trouble. In 799 Pope Leo III was attacked in Rome by his enemies. He escaped and fled north to Charlemagne, who had him restored as pope. So a conquering king and a pope who owed him his job were about to meet again in Rome.

cards.headline: Christmas Day, 800
cards.body: At Christmas mass in St Peter’s Basilica, Leo crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans. For the first time since the empire in the West dissolved in the 5th century (Level 1’s 476), the West had an emperor again. His biographer Einhard later claimed Charlemagne would not have set foot in church that day had he known the pope’s plan. Historians still argue over whether to believe him.

mascot.line: Two emperors both calling themselves Roman. Imagine the seating plan at that dinner.

cards.headline: Who gets to make an emperor?
cards.body: The coronation set a precedent: from then on, emperors in the West would be crowned by popes. Not everyone applauded. In Constantinople, whose people called themselves Romans (Level 4), the Byzantines saw Charlemagne as a usurper of their emperor’s title. A long rivalry between East and West followed. Two emperors, one Roman title. Awkward.

cards.headline: Split three ways
cards.body: The empire didn’t stay whole for long. In 843 the Treaty of Verdun split it among three of Charlemagne’s grandsons. Sound familiar? Clovis’s kingdom was divided among his four sons in Level 6. The lines drawn at Verdun foreshadowed the countries of western Europe, France among them.

title: Who the Vikings Were
objective: After this level you can describe the Vikings as raiders, traders and settlers.
summary: Vikings were Scandinavians who raided, traded and settled from 793. Most were farmers, and they never wore horned helmets.

cards.headline: Picture a Viking. Now take the horns off the helmet.
cards.body: They were never there. The real Vikings were raiders, yes, but also farmers, traders and settlers. Their story starts with a shock on an English island.

cards.headline: 793: terror from the sea
cards.body: The Viking Age is usually dated from 8 June 793, when raiders struck the monastery on Lindisfarne, an island off north-east England. It was the first documented Viking attack. Monasteries made tempting targets: they held church silver and were less well defended than trading towns. Alcuin, Level 11’s scholar, was at Charlemagne’s court when the news arrived. He wrote that never before had such terror appeared in Britain.

cards.headline: Farmers first
cards.body: So who were they? Vikings were Scandinavians, from what are now Denmark, Norway and Sweden, active from the late 8th century to the 11th. Most were farmers, living in villages of six or seven farms. Abroad they could be raiders, but also traders, explorers, settlers or soldiers for hire. Viking traders even brought home silver coins minted in Muslim Central Asia, carried along the rivers of Russia. The axe was one tool in a busy toolkit.

mascot.line: Horns on a crowded ship sound like a great way to annoy the rower behind you.

cards.headline: The helmet problem
cards.body: Now, those horns. The best-preserved Viking Age helmet, from a warrior’s grave at Gjermundbu in Norway, has no horns at all. No writer of the Viking Age mentions horned helmets, and horns would have snagged in a fight or on a crowded ship. The horned look was popularized by 19th-century artists. It’s a costume, not a clue.

title: Viking Ships
objective: After this level you can explain what made Viking longships so fast and flexible.
summary: Clinker-built longships with a square sail and oars drew under a metre of water, so they could run onto beaches, go up rivers and be dragged overland.

cards.headline: “Nor was it thought that such an inroad from the sea could be made.”
cards.body: Alcuin wrote that after Lindisfarne. Viking ships could turn up where nobody expected a ship at all. Here’s how.

cards.headline: Built to take a beating
cards.body: A longship was clinker-built: its planks overlapped, like the shingles on a roof, and were fastened together. The result was sturdy enough for heavy seas. The hull was pointed at both ends, and the ship carried one large square sail plus oars. Sail when the wind helps, row when it doesn’t.

mascot.line: Under a metre! You could wade out to it without getting your shoulders wet.

cards.headline: Less than a metre of water
cards.body: A Viking ship museum built a full-size copy of a warship made near Dublin around 1042: the Sea Stallion, 30 metres long. It needs less than a metre of water. That shallow draught let Viking ships work in shallow water and on rivers. Crews could sail right onto a beach, and even drag their ships over land. No harbour? No problem.

cards.headline: Wind or no wind
cards.body: Under sail, the Sea Stallion has an estimated top speed of 17 knots. When the wind dies, its 60 oars keep it moving. In 2007 and 2008 a modern crew sailed it from Roskilde to Dublin and back to test what these ships could do. Put it together and you get Alcuin’s shock: a raid that arrives from the open sea, with no harbour needed.

title: Vikings Across the World
objective: After this level you can trace Viking voyages from Russia to North America.
summary: Vikings went east along Russian rivers to Kyiv and Constantinople, and west to Iceland, Greenland and Newfoundland, where tree rings show they were in 1021.

cards.headline: Wood cut by Vikings in Newfoundland has been dated to one exact year: 1021.
cards.body: How do you date a wood chip to a single year? And how did Vikings reach North America at all? Follow them west, but first, east.

cards.headline: East: rivers to Constantinople
cards.body: Swedish Vikings controlled a trade route along the rivers of Russia. Around 882 the Viking Oleg, ruler of Novgorod, made Kyiv his capital, founding the state called Kyivan Rus. From Kyiv, merchants took convoys down the Dnieper River to Constantinople, hauling their ships overland around its rapids. Level 4’s great city sat at the end of a Viking trade road.

cards.headline: West: island by island
cards.body: Westward, Norse settlers, most from Norway, settled Iceland in about 870 to 930. About 985, Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, founded the first European settlement on Greenland. He picked the name Greenland believing a good name would attract settlers. Medieval marketing. About 1000, his son Leif Erikson reached North America, and the sagas say he called part of it Vinland.

cards.headline: The year 1021
cards.body: At L’Anse aux Meadows, on the northern tip of Newfoundland, lies the first known evidence of Europeans in the Americas: a Norse camp of timber-and-sod buildings. In 2021 Margot Kuitems and colleagues studied wood cut there with metal tools, which local peoples didn’t make then. A cosmic-ray event in 993 left a spike in that year’s tree ring. Counting outward from it, wood from three trees all gave 1021: Vikings in the Americas, centuries before Columbus.

title: Alfred the Great
objective: After this level you can explain how Alfred defended Wessex against the Vikings.
summary: Alfred of Wessex (871-899) survived the Viking attack of 878, won at Edington, agreed a Danelaw border and defended Wessex with burhs, ships and learning.

cards.headline: In 878 a king of Wessex was hiding in a marsh. He became “Alfred the Great”.
cards.body: He is the only English monarch known as “the Great”. He had lost almost everything to a Viking army. Here’s how he won it back.

cards.headline: Down to the marshes
cards.body: A great Danish army arrived in England in 865. Alfred became king of Wessex, one of Level 9’s Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, in 871. In early 878 the Danes seized Chippenham, and the West Saxons submitted, all except Alfred. He withdrew to the Somerset marshes and fought on. The famous tale of him letting a peasant woman’s cakes burn there? A legend, first written down long after his death.

cards.headline: Edington, then a border
cards.body: In May 878 Alfred beat the Danes at Edington. Their leader, Guthrum, was baptized a Christian with Alfred as his godfather. In 886 Alfred and the Danes agreed a frontier along the old Roman road, Watling Street. The Danish-ruled north and east became known as the Danelaw, “Danes’ law”. The Vikings were no longer just raiders. They were neighbours.

mascot.line: Walls, ships and books. Alfred defended Wessex with all three.

cards.headline: Never more than 20 miles
cards.body: Then Alfred built. He covered Wessex with fortified towns called burhs, placed so that no part of the kingdom was more than 20 miles from one. He had a navy of fast new ships built. And he had Latin books translated into English, taking part in the work himself. Wessex was never again in such danger.

title: The Normans
objective: After this level you can explain who the Normans were and where they settled.
summary: In 911 the Frankish king gave the Viking Rollo land around Rouen. His Northmen became French-speaking Christian Normans and later won lands as far as Sicily.

cards.headline: Normandy is named after Vikings: the Northmen who settled there.
cards.body: Yet their descendants spoke French and went to church. How did a band of raiders turn into a French duchy?

cards.headline: A deal on the Seine
cards.body: Viking raids battered the Frankish coasts in the 9th century, and by about 900 Vikings had a permanent base in the Seine valley. In 911 King Charles III, known as Charles the Simple, made a deal with their leader, Rollo: the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte. Rollo got the land around Rouen and the mouth of the Seine. In return, he stopped raiding, became a Christian and swore loyalty to Charles. The raider became a landholder.

cards.headline: Northmen into Normans
cards.body: Rollo’s Scandinavian countrymen followed in large numbers. Latin writers called them Nortmanni, “Northmen”, which gave us Norman and Normandy. The settlers adopted the French language, French customs and the Christian religion. The Vikings of the Seine became French-speaking Christians with a Norse family story.

mascot.line: From longships on the Seine to a crown in Sicily. Restless family.

cards.headline: Far beyond Normandy
cards.body: The Normans didn’t stay put. Norman adventurers won lands in southern Italy and Sicily, where Roger II became king of Sicily in 1130. And one duke of Normandy had his eye on an even bigger prize. That’s the next level.

cards.headline: In 1066 England had three kings and fought two invading armies in three weeks.
cards.body: Edward, Harold and William all wore the crown that year. Harold had to fight in the north, then race to the south coast. Here’s how it unfolded.

cards.headline: One crown, three claimants
cards.body: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066, and Harold Godwinson was crowned king. Two men disagreed. William, duke of Normandy, claimed Edward had promised him the throne. Harald Hardrada, king of Norway, invaded the north with Harold’s own brother, Tostig.

cards.headline: North, then south
cards.body: On 25 September Harold beat the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, near York. Hardrada and Tostig were both killed. The battle is traditionally taken as the end of the Viking Age. Three days later, on 28 September, William’s fleet landed at Pevensey on the south coast. Harold marched south to meet him.

mascot.line: A famous arrow that may be mostly 19th-century thread. Always check the stitches!

cards.headline: Hastings, 14 October
cards.body: The armies met near Hastings on 14 October 1066 and fought all day. Late in the afternoon Harold was killed, and the English fled. How he died is debated. The Bayeux Tapestry, really an embroidery about 68 metres long, seems to show an arrow in his eye, but that arrow was added in 19th-century repairs. The accounts written nearest the battle suggest Norman knights cut him down.

cards.headline: Christmas Day, again
cards.body: William was crowned king in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066. Remember Charlemagne’s Christmas crowning in Level 12? And Level 9’s Anglo-Saxon rule was over.

title: The Domesday Book
objective: After this level you can explain why William the Conqueror surveyed all of England.
summary: At Christmas 1085 William ordered a survey of who held England's land and what it was worth; the 1086 results became Domesday Book.

cards.headline: Nineteen years after Hastings, William wanted to count every pig in England.
cards.body: Or so it felt to the English. The result names more than 13,000 places, and most of them still exist.

cards.headline: Christmas 1085
cards.body: At Christmas 1085 William ordered a survey of England, and it was carried out the following year. Why? He needed to fix problems in how tax was raised and how defence was organised. That meant knowing who held what land, and what it was worth. Nearly twenty years into his reign, he still didn’t know exactly who held what.

cards.headline: Who? How many? What’s it worth?
cards.body: Commissioners asked the same questions everywhere. Who held this manor under King Edward, and who holds it now? How many plough teams and mills? What was it worth in 1066, and what now? The answers showed how England had changed since the Conquest. One writer of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle complained that not one ox, cow or pig was left out. Picture a tax inspector with a clipboard, times a whole kingdom.

mascot.line: A survey so final they named it after Judgement Day. Tough crowd.

cards.headline: A book with no appeal
cards.body: The results fill Domesday Book, which names more than 13,000 places, though London and Winchester were left out. People at the time called it the description of England. By the mid-12th century it had a scarier name: Domesday, after the Day of Judgement, because its record could not be appealed. It is kept today at The National Archives.

title: Feudalism
objective: After this level you can explain how lords, vassals and land were tied together.
summary: Lords granted vassals fiefs, usually land, for service, sealed by homage and fealty. The word feudalism came centuries later, and the tidy pyramid is a simplification.

cards.headline: Nobody in the Middle Ages ever talked about “feudalism”.
cards.body: The word was coined centuries later. The deal it describes was real, though: land in return for loyalty and service. Here’s how it worked, and why historians argue about the label.

cards.headline: Land for service
cards.body: A lord granted a vassal a fief: a piece of property, usually land, held in return for service. The vassal owed his lord military service, counsel and financial support. The lord, in return, was expected to protect and respect him. In England the king granted land in return for “knight service”, because a knight’s armour and heavy horse were expensive to buy and keep. No wages, no payslip: you got land, and you turned up armed when called.

cards.headline: Becoming someone’s man
cards.body: The bond was sealed in a ceremony called homage, in which the vassal became the lord’s “man”. The word comes from Latin homo, “man”. He also swore fealty, a promise to be faithful. So this wasn’t a company hiring an employee. It was two people, bound by an oath.
cards.callout: Homage: becoming his man. Fealty: swearing to be faithful.

mascot.line: A tidy triangle is easy to draw. Medieval Europe was never quite that tidy.

cards.headline: Handle the pyramid with care
cards.body: You may have seen it drawn as a pyramid: king on top, then lords, knights and peasants. Treat that as a simplification, because arrangements differed widely across Europe. In 1974 the historian Elizabeth A. R. Brown argued that feudalism has no agreed definition and is misleading. In 1994 Susan Reynolds argued that words like fief and vassal had no precise technical meaning until lawyers defined them in the late 12th century. Many historians now avoid the term.

title: Serfs and Peasants
objective: After this level you can describe the life of a medieval peasant.
summary: A serf was bound to a hereditary plot and to his lord's will. Villeins worked the lord's demesne every week and paid in produce and fees, from the lord's mill to merchet and heriot.

cards.headline: A serf wasn’t a slave. He still couldn’t move house without permission.
cards.body: He was bound to a plot of land and to the will of his lord. So what exactly was a serf, and what did he owe?

mascot.line: Not owned, but not free to leave either. Serfdom lived in that awkward middle.

cards.headline: Tied to the land
cards.body: A serf held a hereditary plot of land, and he was bound to it and to his lord. That’s the difference from a slave: slaves were bought and sold without reference to land, while a serf went with his plot. He could not leave his holding or village for good, marry, or change his occupation without his lord’s permission. The ways out were few: being formally freed by the lord, or running away.

cards.headline: Working the lord’s land
cards.body: Every manor had a demesne, the part the lord kept for his own use, and serfs supplied the labour to work it. Week by week an unfree peasant, a villein, brought his own plough and oxen to plough the demesne, then harrowed, reaped, threshed and carried the crops. This duty was called week-work. His own holding, a cottage and some strips of land in the fields, had to fit around it. Picture paying your rent by doing your landlord’s gardening every single week.

cards.headline: A bill for everything
cards.body: A villein paid for his holding in money, labour and produce. A substantial share of the grain a serf grew went to his lord, and he had to use his lord’s mill. Marrying off a daughter cost a fee called merchet. And when he died, his family owed the lord a heriot, usually the best beast. Even dying came with a bill.

title: Castles
objective: After this level you can explain how castles were built and why.
summary: A castle was a king's or lord's fortified home. Early motte-and-bailey castles were quick earth-and-timber works; by the 12th century lords built stone keeps.

cards.headline: Some early castle towers arrived more or less flat-packed.
cards.body: Timber towers were often made off-site, then put up on top of a mound of earth. So what was a castle for, and how did wood turn into stone?

cards.headline: A home that could fight back
cards.body: A castle was a medieval stronghold, generally the home of the king or lord of the land around it. Castles developed rapidly in western Europe from the 9th century. In England they were something new after the Norman Conquest of 1066: they housed Norman nobles and their families, as well as knights and soldiers, and helped the Normans control the land they had conquered. Part house, part barracks, part statement: we’re staying.

mascot.line: An upside-down pudding bowl with a tower on top. Not delicious, but very hard to attack.

cards.headline: A mound and a yard
cards.body: The common early design was the motte and bailey. The motte was an artificial mound of earth and stone, shaped like an upside-down pudding bowl and topped by a timber tower. Beside it lay the bailey, a fenced yard with houses and animal pens. Unskilled forced labourers could build one quickly from basic materials, and the towers were often prefabricated off-site, then put up like enormous flat-pack furniture. Some assembly required.

cards.headline: From timber to stone
cards.body: Stone gave better defence and more prestige, so earth and timber gave way to stone. By the 12th century lords were building stone keeps, much easier to defend than wooden towers, some with walls six metres thick. The keep was the strongest part of the castle, with a well, private rooms and supplies for a siege. It sent a message: this lord is rich, and he isn’t going anywhere.

title: Castle Defenses
objective: After this level you can explain how moats, walls, towers and gatehouses kept attackers out.
summary: Moats, curtain walls and arrow loops held attackers off; gatehouses with portcullises and murder holes made the way in a trap; concentric castles like Beaumaris layered it all.

cards.headline: Murder holes: the name tells you exactly what they were for.
cards.body: Castle builders turned the way in into the most dangerous place to stand. Let’s walk through a castle’s defences from the outside in.

cards.headline: The outer ring
cards.body: Start with the moat, crossed by a drawbridge hinged at one end so it could be raised. Behind it rose the curtain wall, a fortified wall linking the towers together. Narrow vertical slits called arrow loops let archers shoot out while staying safe behind stone. Anyone attacking was out in the open. The defenders were not.

mascot.line: Castle rule: the friendlier the doorway looks, the more you should worry.

cards.headline: The gate is a trap
cards.body: The gate was a castle’s most vulnerable point, so gatehouses often became mini-castles in themselves. A portcullis, a heavy wooden or iron grille, could drop to seal the passage. Overhead were murder holes, openings through which defenders dropped heavy stones, hot sand or boiling water on anyone below. Get past the front door, and you were standing in the worst room in the house.

cards.headline: Walls within walls
cards.body: The most powerful design was the concentric castle: two rings of towered walls, one inside the other, each supporting the other. At Beaumaris in Wales, Edward I and his architect James of St George built four rings of defences, including a water-filled moat with its own dock. The outer walls alone had 300 arrow loops. Then the money ran out, and work petered out by the 1320s, unfinished. Remember Constantinople’s moat and layered walls in Level 4? Same idea: make attackers win again and again.

title: Siege Warfare
objective: After this level you can explain how armies besieged castles, from ladders to trebuchets.
summary: Attackers used ladders, towers, rams, mines and trebuchets, yet most sieges ended by treachery, starvation or disease, as at Rochester in 1215 after a pig-fat mine.

cards.headline: In 1215 King John sent for 40 pigs too fat to eat.
cards.body: He wasn’t planning a feast. He was besieging Rochester Castle, held against him by rebels. To see why he wanted pig fat, start with the attacker’s toolkit.

cards.headline: Over, through or under
cards.body: Attackers could climb the walls with ladders, but this escalade rarely worked except by surprise or treachery. Wheeled wooden siege towers could roll up and drop a drawbridge onto the wall. Battering rams, sheltered by a wheeled shed, went for the gate. Or miners dug a tunnel under the wall, propped it with timber, packed it with fuel and set it alight, so the wall above collapsed.

mascot.line: Forty unappetising pigs, one collapsed corner. Medieval engineering could be very creative.

cards.headline: The pig-fat mine
cards.body: That was John’s plan. His siege engines bombarded Rochester’s keep with stones while miners attacked its south-east turret from below. They burned the fat of the 40 pigs to fire the timber props, and the south-east corner of the keep came down. Even then the rebels didn’t give up: they fell back into the northern half of the keep. The king had brought down the wall, but not the defenders.

cards.headline: The slowest weapon wins
cards.body: The trebuchet was a throwing engine powered by a falling counterweight. Counterweight engines appeared in the 12th century and could hurl stones weighing hundreds of kilograms. Yet medieval sieges were settled more often by treachery, starvation or disease than by broken walls. Rochester ended the same way: starvation soon forced the rebels to surrender. Sometimes the deadliest siege weapon was a calendar.

title: Becoming a Knight
objective: After this level you can explain how a boy trained to become a knight.
summary: A noble boy served as a page from about 7, joined his father's lord's household at about 12, and trained as a squire before being dubbed with the accolade, if he could afford the equipment.

cards.headline: Becoming a knight could start at about the age of 7.
cards.body: Long before a sword touched his shoulder, a boy of noble birth spent years serving, learning and carrying other people’s gear. Here’s the road, step by step.

cards.headline: Step one: page
cards.body: A boy destined for knighthood might serve as a page from about the age of 7. At around 12 he joined the household of his father’s lord for further training. At this stage he might be called a damoiseau, literally “lordling”. Think of it as boarding school with horses, where the head teacher was your father’s lord.

cards.headline: Step two: squire
cards.body: Next he served as a squire: a young man of noble birth, apprenticed in the duties of chivalry, who looked after a knight’s armour and weapons. The training went well beyond fighting, taking in hunting, music and dancing. The goal was a worthy knight, a just master and a sensible manager of an estate. Swordplay, dance steps and estate accounts: a demanding timetable.

mascot.line: Years of training, and the big moment is a tap on the shoulder. Knights did understatement well.

cards.headline: Step three: the accolade
cards.body: When he was skilled enough, and had the money, he was dubbed. The accolade was a touch on the shoulder with the flat of a sword blade. But he had to buy his own knightly equipment, and in France some squires waited for, or put off, the expensive dubbing. Many knights were vassals holding lands as fiefs from the lords they fought for. Remember Level 21’s land-for-service deal? These are the men who turned up.

title: Armor
objective: After this level you can explain how armor changed from chain mail to plate.
summary: Mail of iron links gave way to plate from the late 13th century, fast after 1325. Field armour weighed about 20 to 25 kg, and the crane is a film myth.

cards.headline: Knights were never winched onto their horses by crane.
cards.body: That picture comes from films, such as the 1944 Henry V. Real armour had to let a man fight. So what was it made of, and how heavy was it?

cards.headline: A shirt of rings
cards.body: Before plate, the standard metal armour across Europe was mail: a flexible mesh of interlocking iron links, worn over a quilted garment. A mail shirt, or hauberk, contained thousands of links and was expensive and slow to make. It moved with the body and stopped sword cuts well, but it was less good against arrows and blows from maces. Think of a knitted jumper, made of iron.

cards.headline: Enter the plates
cards.body: Plate armour emerged in the late 13th century. Between 1325 and 1340 came a revolution: mail was replaced or reinforced with plates of iron or steel. Through the 14th century, plates spread to the rest of the body, until the complete suit, the harness, was developed. Rigid plates deflected glancing blows; a weapon got through only if it struck directly and with great force.

mascot.line: No cranes, no winches, no being stuck on your back like a beetle. Just practice.

cards.fact: A field armour usually weighed about 20 to 25 kg.
cards.context: That weight was spread over the whole body. Even a suddenly unhorsed knight could get up quickly, ready to fight, and modern tests show a man in properly fitted armour can mount a horse, lie on the ground and stand up again. Heavy, yes. Helpless, no.

title: Chivalry
objective: After this level you can explain the ideals of chivalry and how far knights lived up to them.
summary: Chivalry first meant mounted knights, then an ideal of faith, loyalty and honour. In practice mercy was mostly for ransomable nobles.

cards.headline: “Chivalry” first meant men on horses, not good manners.
cards.body: In the Middle Ages the word meant knights: fully armed, mounted fighting men. Only later did it come to mean courtesy. The gap between those two meanings is this level’s story.

cards.headline: The ideal
cards.body: By the 12th and 13th centuries, chivalry meant the honourable, courteous conduct expected of a knight. A Christian ideal took hold: respect the Church, protect the poor and the weak, stay loyal to your superiors, and guard your personal honour. It’s the knight of the storybooks. And that’s the catch: it was an ideal.

cards.headline: The reality
cards.body: Real knights fought pragmatically. A captured enemy knight might be spared if he was worth land, gold or booty, not out of kindness, and ransoms and plunder could bring great profits. That protection didn’t reach peasants, who were often slaughtered when they got in the way. Chivalry was built around the noble warrior on horseback, and peasants weren’t in the club.

mascot.line: An ideal is worth knowing. Just check it against what people actually did.

cards.headline: Part of the problem
cards.body: Some historians go further. In 1999 Richard Kaeuper argued that chivalry was part of the problem of violence in medieval Europe, not merely its solution. Chivalric writing prized prowess, skill at violent deeds, so highly that it became almost a one-word definition of chivalry, even as the Church tried to regulate knightly violence. The code was real. So was the gap.

title: Heraldry
objective: After this level you can explain coats of arms and what they told people.
summary: Heraldry took shape in the 12th century to tell armoured men apart. Coats of arms, named after the surcoat, used set metals and colours, a rule of contrast, and became hereditary.

cards.headline: In 1127 a king hung a shield of golden lions around a young man’s neck.
cards.body: Henry I of England gave the blue shield to Geoffrey of Anjou, his future son-in-law. It’s an early glimpse of heraldry. So why did knights need pictures on their shields?

cards.headline: Who’s in there?
cards.body: As armour came to cover the whole body, telling one armoured man from another got harder, and that sped the spread of heraldry. It took shape in the 12th century, and by about 1170 heralds appear in descriptions of tournaments. A design on a shield worked like a name tag you could read from across a field.

mascot.line: Gold on blue: easy to spot across a muddy field. Blue on black: good luck.

cards.headline: A coat of arms, literally
cards.body: The phrase “coat of arms” comes from the surcoat, a cloth tunic worn over armour that displayed the bearer’s arms. Heraldry had its own colour names: the metals gold (or) and silver (argent), and colours such as red (gules), blue (azure) and black (sable). A rule of contrast generally kept colour off colour and metal off metal, so a design stayed visible. Geoffrey’s gold lions on blue passed the test.

cards.headline: Handed down
cards.body: Over time, arms tended to become hereditary, passing down through families. A design that once said “this is the man” came to say “this is the family”. A shield had become a surname you could see.

title: The Medieval Church
objective: After this level you can explain the Church's power over daily life.
summary: The parish church was the one place for the sacraments and burial, the tithe took a tenth of everyone's income, and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) required yearly confession.

cards.headline: In a medieval village, the biggest building was often the church.
cards.body: It was also the one building that mattered to every parishioner, whatever their age or wealth. What made one building so central to ordinary life?

cards.headline: From the font to the grave
cards.body: Your whole life ran through that building. Apart from the last anointing of the dying, the parish church was normally the only place you could receive the sacraments, and it was where you would be buried. In the 12th century the theologian Peter Lombard, whose textbook became the standard one, counted seven sacraments, including baptism, marriage and the Eucharist. Baptized, married, buried: one address for all three.

mascot.line: One sheaf in ten, every year. Suddenly a phone bill looks rather gentle.

cards.headline: A tenth of everything
cards.body: The Church also took a share of your income. The tithe was a tenth of it, paid in money or in crops and farm animals. Church law required it from the 6th century, and from the 8th, kings’ law enforced it across Europe. It paid the clergy, kept churches standing and helped the poor. Picture handing over one sheaf of wheat in every ten you cut, every single year.

cards.headline: Once a year, by order
cards.body: In 1215 Pope Innocent III gathered more than 400 bishops and 800 abbots and priors at the Fourth Lateran Council. One of its rules reached every believer: each Catholic had to confess at least once a year and take Communion during Lent. The Church now set a date in everyone’s calendar. A yearly check-up for the soul, and not an optional one.

title: Popes and Emperors
objective: After this level you can explain the struggle between popes and emperors over power.
summary: In the Investiture Controversy, Gregory VII excommunicated Henry IV, who sought absolution at Canossa in 1077; the Concordat of Worms (1122) split the rights to install bishops.

cards.headline: In January 1077, a king crossed the Alps in winter to beg a pope’s forgiveness.
cards.body: He waited three days at a castle called Canossa before the pope let him back into the Church. How did a pope get that kind of power over a king?

cards.headline: Who hands over the ring?
cards.body: The fight was over investiture: who installs a new bishop. Traditionally the king did it, handing the bishop a ring and a crosier, the shepherd’s staff, with the words “receive the church”. Those objects stood for the spiritual office and for the lands and property that came with it. Whoever held the ring and staff held a lot of power. Kings wanted it. So did popes.

cards.headline: Pope against king
cards.body: In 1075 Pope Gregory VII set out sweeping claims for his office, including that a pope could depose emperors. In January 1076 the German king Henry IV and his bishops told Gregory to step down. Gregory struck back in February: he deposed Henry and excommunicated him, the first pope to depose a crowned ruler. Excommunication shut a person out of the sacraments, the very rites Level 31’s parish church existed to give.

cards.headline: Three days at Canossa
cards.body: So Henry submitted. He went to Canossa as a penitent and, as tradition tells it, stood barefoot in the snow for three days. On January 28 Gregory absolved him. Centuries later, during Prussia’s struggle with the Catholic Church, Otto von Bismarck declared, “We are not going to Canossa.” One castle had become shorthand for backing down.

mascot.line: Ring for the Church, land for the ruler. Every good compromise leaves both sides a little grumpy.

cards.headline: The deal at Worms
cards.body: The quarrel outlived both men. In 1122 the Concordat of Worms split the difference: the emperor Henry V gave up investing bishops with ring and crosier and accepted their free election, but kept the right to invest them with their lands. The Church got the ring. The ruler kept the real estate.

title: Building Cathedrals
objective: After this level you can explain how medieval builders raised huge cathedrals.
summary: Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let Gothic cathedrals rise and fill with windows; master masons and treadwheel cranes built them, partly paid for by tithes.

cards.headline: Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248. It was finished in 1880.
cards.body: That’s 632 years from first stone to last, with a pause of centuries in the middle. How do you build something that takes longer than a lifetime?

cards.headline: Stone that pushes sideways
cards.body: A stone ceiling is heavy, and a vault pushes outward on the walls beneath it. Gothic builders answered with three tools. The pointed arch and the rib vault, where stone ribs carry the ceiling, let them cover taller, broader spaces. The flying buttress, a half arch, carried the vault’s thrust across an aisle to an outer pier. With the push handled outside, walls could open into huge windows. Tradition names Saint-Denis, rebuilt about 1135 to 1144 under Abbot Suger, as the first Gothic building.

cards.headline: The master mason’s building site
cards.body: A master mason ran the site. He made templates for every shaped stone and put a master craftsman in charge of each part of the job. Canterbury’s builders brought stone by boat from France, easier than hauling it over bad roads. On scaffolding, cranes and pulleys lifted it, some powered by a treadwheel: a “hamster wheel” big enough for two men. And the bills? Tithes were a prime source of money for many great cathedrals.

mascot.line: Nobody was taking the stairs that day. Engineering is learned, sometimes the hard way.

title: Pilgrimage
objective: After this level you can explain why people went on pilgrimages and where they went.
summary: Pilgrims travelled for penance, cures, vows and salvation, to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and Canterbury, where Becket's murder in 1170 created a great shrine.

cards.headline: A medieval traveller home from Spain might wear a scallop shell.
cards.body: Not a beach souvenir. The scallop was the emblem of St James and his shrine at Santiago de Compostela. Why did so many people set off on journeys like that?

cards.headline: Why go?
cards.body: Medieval Christians went on pilgrimage for many reasons: to seek salvation, to fulfil a vow, to do penance for their sins, or in hope of a miraculous cure. At the greatest shrines, Jerusalem and Rome, pilgrims could also gain indulgences, which the Church taught remitted the penalty of sin. One journey could be a prayer, a punishment and a hospital visit at once.

cards.headline: A shell to prove it
cards.body: After Jerusalem and Rome came Santiago de Compostela in Spain, where the apostle James’s body was believed to have been brought. Pilgrims wore badges from the shrines they reached, on their necks, clothes or bags, and the scallop was James’s. Many believed a saint’s power passed into a souvenir that had touched the shrine. Some even buried them in house foundations for protection.

cards.headline: A murder makes a shrine
cards.body: On December 29, 1170, Archbishop Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral by four knights. By 1173 he was a saint, and a whole industry grew up around the pilgrims coming to his shrine. Two centuries later, Chaucer built The Canterbury Tales (1387–1400) around 30 pilgrims travelling there from Southwark, holding a storytelling contest on the way. A famous poem, and at heart a road trip.

title: Monks and Nuns
objective: After this level you can describe daily life in a monastery or convent.
summary: Monks and nuns lived by the Divine Office, eight services from matins in the night to compline, around a cloister; nuns lived the same pattern under abbesses in small, enclosed houses.

cards.headline: Imagine an alarm that goes off eight times a day, starting in the night.
cards.body: For medieval monks and nuns, that was simply the timetable. Level 7 gave you Benedict’s Rule. Now step inside the day it made.

cards.headline: The Divine Office
cards.body: The backbone of the day was the Divine Office: psalms, hymns, prayers and readings at set hours. Matins, the longest, came at night. Prime came early, lauds and vespers were the great morning and evening prayers, terce, sext and none marked mid-morning, noon and mid-afternoon, and compline was the night prayer. Remember Benedict’s balance of prayer, work and reading? The Office was the prayer. The work and study fitted in between.

cards.headline: A world around a square
cards.body: Life centered on the cloister, a square enclosure ringed by covered walkways. In a Benedictine house the church stood on one side and the refectory, the dining hall, faced it; the chapter house sat on the east and the dormitory upstairs. Young members were taught in the cloister and elders studied there. It was also for exercise, and its walks were where the dead were buried. School, gym and graveyard, all around one square.

cards.headline: Nuns and abbesses
cards.body: Women lived this life too. An abbess was the superior of a community of nuns following the Benedictine Rule, and some abbesses even ruled double monasteries of monks and nuns. An English nun’s day had the same three parts: eight services, devotional reading and manual labour. Strict enclosure kept nuns inside the walls, and most English houses were small: only a minority had more than a dozen or so nuns.

title: Hildegard of Bingen
objective: After this level you can describe Hildegard's music, writing and science.
summary: Hildegard of Bingen (born 1098), a German abbess, recorded her visions in Scivias, composed songs and the Ordo virtutum, wrote on medicine and corresponded with popes and an emperor.

cards.headline: In a 12th-century play, every character sings except one: the Devil.
cards.body: He only speaks, because the author believed the Devil had no divine harmony. She was Hildegard of Bingen, a German abbess who also wrote about medicine and traded letters with popes.

cards.headline: From pupil to leader
cards.body: Hildegard was born in 1098 and educated by a woman named Jutta at the Benedictine cloister of Disibodenberg. She took the Benedictine habit at 15, and in 1136 she succeeded Jutta as prioress. About 1147 she left with several nuns to found her own convent at Rupertsberg, near Bingen. Pupil, prioress, founder: three steps in one life.

cards.headline: Visions on the page
cards.body: At 43 she told her confessor about the visions she experienced. The result was Scivias (1141–52), a book describing 26 of them. She also travelled widely through Germany, preaching about her visions to large crowds. A nun, speaking in public, to anyone who would listen.

mascot.line: Poor Devil. All that scheming and not a single tune.

cards.headline: A composer with a Devil problem
cards.body: She collected 77 of her poems, each set to music she composed herself. Her Ordo virtutum, the Play of the Virtues, is the earliest known morality play: 17 Virtues, sung by women, fight for a human soul, while the Devil can only speak. In Hildegard’s world, evil is tone-deaf.

cards.headline: Healer, letter-writer, saint
cards.body: At Rupertsberg she cared for the sick and wrote two medical works: Causes and Cures, on theory, and Physica, full of remedies. About 390 of her letters survive, to popes, an emperor, kings, queens and ordinary lay people. In 2012 the Catholic Church made her a saint and a Doctor of the Church. Nine centuries on, still collecting titles.

title: The First Universities
objective: After this level you can explain how the first universities began.
summary: Universities began as guilds of students and masters: Bologna late in the 11th century, Paris between 1150 and 1170, and Oxford by 1200. They taught a spherical Earth from Sacrobosco's Sphere.

cards.headline: The first universities weren’t buildings. They were groups of people.
cards.body: Students and teachers banded together, a bit like a trade guild, and popes, emperors and kings gave them charters. How did a crowd of scholars become an institution?

cards.headline: Bologna: a union of outsiders
cards.body: The first true university in the West grew up at Bologna, in Italy, late in the 11th century, and it became the leading school of canon and civil law. Scholars who weren’t citizens of Bologna formed guilds by nationality to secure protections the city didn’t give them. In 1158 the emperor Frederick I granted them privileges, later extended to all Italian universities. Think of it as a union for out-of-towners.

cards.headline: Paris and Oxford
cards.body: Northern Europe’s first university, Paris, was founded between 1150 and 1170 and became famous for theology. Oxford was well established by the end of the 12th century. These were studia generalia: recognized places of study open to students from all over Europe. A student from Scotland and one from Sicily could sit in the same lecture.

mascot.line: Nobody in that lecture hall was worried about sailing off the edge.

cards.headline: A round Earth on the syllabus
cards.body: One thing they taught: the Earth is a sphere. Around 1230 Johannes de Sacrobosco, who taught at Paris, wrote The Sphere, which became the most popular university astronomy textbook. It argued at length that the Earth is round. It circulated in handwritten copies for 240 years, then was printed from 1476. The idea that medieval people thought the Earth was flat is a myth spread by 19th-century writers.

title: The Great Schism
objective: After this level you can explain why the Church split into East and West in 1054.
summary: In 1054 a papal legate and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other, the traditional date of the East-West split, after centuries of drifting apart.

cards.headline: In 1054 a cardinal walked into Hagia Sophia and excommunicated a patriarch.
cards.body: It was July 16, and the pope who had sent him was already dead. Did one day in July really split Christianity in two?

cards.headline: Excommunication, returned
cards.body: Remember Justinian’s great church from Level 5? That’s where it happened. The papal legate Cardinal Humbert excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius and his clergy. Cerularius called a synod and excommunicated the pope’s envoys right back. These mutual excommunications became a watershed in church history, the traditional date for the split between the Latin West and the Orthodox East. A slammed door, heard for centuries.

cards.headline: Drifting apart
cards.body: But the two churches had been drifting apart since the 5th century. The East never accepted Rome’s growing claim to lead the whole Church. Rome had added “and the Son” to the Creed without consulting the East. Easterners also resented Roman rules on celibate clergy and unleavened bread at the Eucharist. And Level 4’s eastern empire had swapped Latin for Greek in government. 1054 was less an explosion than the end of a long, slow drift.

mascot.line: Nine centuries to retract a letter. And you thought your inbox was slow.

cards.headline: Undoing 1054
cards.body: The excommunications themselves stood until 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I held simultaneous ceremonies revoking them. That’s 911 years to take back one July’s work.

title: Heresy and the Inquisition
objective: After this level you can explain how the Church dealt with people who disagreed with it.
summary: The Church condemned beliefs like Cathar dualism as heresy. From 1227 papal inquisitors tried suspects; most got penances or prison, and the unrepentant were burned.

cards.headline: An inquisitor arrives in your town with an offer: confess now, get off lightly.
cards.body: That was how a medieval inquiry often began. What came next depended on what you had believed, and what you said.

cards.headline: What counted as heresy
cards.body: Heresy was a belief that church authorities rejected as false. The best-known medieval example was the Cathars, who spread across western Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries. They believed in two principles, one good and one evil, and held that the material world was evil. Their leaders, the perfect, were set apart by a ceremony called the consolamentum. In 1209, under Pope Innocent III, a crusade against them began.

cards.headline: The inquisitors
cards.body: From 1227 Pope Gregory IX appointed the first inquisitors to investigate heresy; many were Dominican and Franciscan friars. An inquisitor opened with a period of grace, when those who confessed got light penances. Then came trials, where suspects usually weren’t told the charges or who had accused them. From 1252 Pope Innocent IV allowed stubborn suspects to be tortured by lay officials.

cards.headline: Penance, prison or the fire
cards.body: Those found guilty might be sent on penitential pilgrimages, made to wear yellow crosses sewn on their clothes, or imprisoned. Those who refused to recant were handed to the secular authorities and burned. At Verona in 1278, more than 150 Cathars were burned together. Such mass burnings were not the usual outcome, though: the inquisitors’ chief aim was to bring heretics back into the Church.

cards.headline: Counting the fires
cards.body: Film has made Bernard Gui, inquisitor of Toulouse, a byword for cruelty. His own records tell a smaller, grimmer story: of the hundreds of people he sentenced, a few dozen were burned. Fewer than legend suggests, and still people, each one, sent to the fire for what they believed.

title: Why the Crusades Began
objective: After this level you can explain Pope Urban II's call in 1095 and why so many answered it.
summary: A Byzantine appeal against the Turks led Urban II to call knights east at Clermont in 1095. Those who went wore a cross and were promised remission of penance for sin.

cards.headline: In 1095 a pope called Western knights to march east. Why did so many go?
cards.body: The Crusades began with a request for help from an old empire and one famous speech at Clermont. Start there.

cards.headline: A request from Constantinople
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s Byzantine Empire, whose people still called themselves Romans? It now faced a dangerous enemy: the Seljuk Turks. So its emperor, Alexius I Comnenus, sent envoys to Pope Urban II with a request: help against the Turks. It was a call for soldiers, the kind of favor you ask a powerful friend. The pope turned it into something much bigger.

cards.headline: The speech at Clermont
cards.body: In November 1095, at a church council in Clermont, in France, Urban urged Western knights to go east and rescue the Holy Land from the Turks. His exact words are lost: the only accounts of the speech were written years later. But the reply was remembered. Cries of “God wills it” rang out, and those who agreed to go were to wear a cross. That cross gave the movement its later name.
cards.callout: Crusade comes from Latin crux, “cross”

cards.headline: Why so many said yes
cards.body: Urban’s council offered a powerful reward. Anyone who went to aid the Christians of the East received a plenary indulgence: the remission of all penance for their sins. Crusaders believed that fighting what they saw as a holy war was a way to win redemption. Imagine being told one hard journey could settle a lifetime of debts. For many who took the cross, that was the promise.

cards.headline: Before it reached the Holy Land, the First Crusade struck the Rhineland’s Jews.
cards.body: Before any army reached Jerusalem, crusader bands turned on the Jewish communities of the Rhineland in 1096. The road to Jerusalem in 1099 starts there.

cards.headline: Spring 1096: the Rhineland
cards.body: In May 1096, crusader bands attacked the Jewish communities of Rhineland towns including Speyer, Worms and Mainz. Many Jews were left only a choice between baptism and death, and some chose death. At Mainz, Jews sheltered in the bishop’s castle, but he fled before the attack, and more than 1,000 were killed. These massacres are traditionally seen as a turning point in Jewish-Christian relations and a pivotal moment in the history of antisemitism.

cards.headline: The long road east
cards.body: Not every band got far. The People’s Crusade, stirred up by the preacher Peter the Hermit, was ambushed and all but wiped out by the Turks in Anatolia in 1096. The main armies did better. After a long siege, they captured the great city of Antioch in June 1098. Jerusalem was next.

cards.headline: Divided rivals
cards.body: Here’s the surprise: the crusaders didn’t face one united Muslim world. The Seljuk empire never held together as a unit, and Shi‘i Fatimid Egypt and Sunni Baghdad were rivals. The Fatimids had even taken Jerusalem for themselves in August 1098. So the crusaders’ final push was against Egypt’s Fatimids, not the Turks that Alexius had asked for help against. Two quarreling neighbors are easier to beat than one.

cards.headline: Jerusalem, 15 July 1099
cards.body: On 15 July 1099 the crusaders stormed Jerusalem. In the slaughter that followed, many of its Muslim and Jewish men, women and children were killed. The city’s Jews had fought beside their Muslim neighbors; they sheltered in synagogues, which the attackers set on fire. Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen to govern and took a modest title, Defender of the Holy Sepulchre. Keep this day in mind: it returns in Level 44.

title: The Crusader States
objective: After this level you can describe the kingdoms the crusaders set up in the Levant.
summary: Four crusader states, called Outremer, were ruled by a Christian minority. Bohemond kept Antioch despite his oath, and Edessa’s fall in 1144 set off a failed Second Crusade.

cards.headline: Europeans called the new crusader lands Outremer: “overseas”.
cards.body: Winning Jerusalem was one thing. Holding a strip of land far from home, surrounded by rivals, was another.

cards.headline: Four states
cards.body: After the First Crusade, the newcomers set up four states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. Europeans called them Outremer, French for “overseas”. Godfrey had settled for a modest title, Defender of the Holy Sepulchre. His brother Baldwin, who had first become ruler of Edessa, took the title of king of Jerusalem in November 1100, after Godfrey died.

cards.headline: A broken promise
cards.body: The Byzantines saw things differently. On the way east, Emperor Alexius had made each crusade leader swear to hand back any conquered land that had belonged to his empire before the Turkish invasions. Bohemond, who had led the capture of Antioch, ignored his oath and kept the city for himself. Alexius had asked for soldiers. He got new neighbors who kept the keys.

cards.headline: A ruling minority
cards.body: Outremer was a set of feudal lands, but its lords were a Christian minority ruling diverse local peoples, including Muslims and many kinds of Christians. Picture a few newcomers taking over a busy city where most people speak other languages and pray in other ways.

cards.headline: The first to fall
cards.body: In 1144 the Muslim ruler Zengi captured Edessa, the northernmost and weakest of the four states. Its loss set off the Second Crusade, led by Louis VII of France and Conrad III of Germany. It failed outside Damascus in 1148, and Edessa was never won back. From then on, the crusader states stayed on the defensive.

title: Saladin
objective: After this level you can explain how Saladin united Muslim forces and retook Jerusalem.
summary: Saladin, a Kurdish commander, united Egypt and Syria, destroyed the crusaders at Hattin in 1187 and took Jerusalem on ransom terms. The West later made him a legend.

cards.headline: In 1187 Jerusalem changed hands again. This time a Kurdish sultan took it.
cards.body: His name was Saladin. The West turned him into a legend of chivalry. The real man is more interesting.

cards.headline: From Tikrit to Cairo
cards.body: Saladin was born in 1137 or 1138 in Tikrit, in today’s Iraq, into a prominent Kurdish family. In 1169, aged 31, he became vizier of Egypt. In 1171 he abolished the Shi‘i Fatimid caliphate, the dynasty that had held Jerusalem in 1099, and returned Egypt to Sunni Islam. From 1174 he spent a dozen years uniting Egypt, Syria, northern Mesopotamia and Palestine. Egypt and Syria were the lands the first caliphs took from Byzantium in Level 8. The divided rivals of Level 42 now had one leader.

cards.headline: Hattin, 4 July 1187
cards.body: Saladin was intensely devoted to jihad, holy war, against the crusaders. On 4 July 1187, at Hattin in northern Palestine, he trapped an exhausted, thirst-stricken crusader army and destroyed it. He spared the captured King Guy and most of the lords. But he ordered the execution of almost all the captured Templars and Hospitallers, the knights of the military orders. Mercy and ruthlessness, on the same day.

cards.headline: Jerusalem, 2 October 1187
cards.body: Three months later, Jerusalem surrendered, after 88 years under the Franks. Saladin had planned to avenge the slaughter of 1099 by killing the city’s Christians. Instead he agreed to let the inhabitants buy their freedom. Several thousand were apparently not ransomed and were probably sold into slavery. Not a massacre, and not a free pass: set beside 1099, the difference is stark.

cards.headline: A legend in the West
cards.body: Western chroniclers praised Saladin as a gallant, chivalrous enemy, and for centuries Western novels and films celebrated his generosity. He died in Damascus in 1193, leaving too little money to pay for his grave. The legend is warm. The real Saladin was devout and determined, and ruthless when he chose to be.

title: Richard the Lionheart
objective: After this level you can describe Richard's role in the Third Crusade.
summary: Richard I took Acre, executed its garrison and won at Arsuf, but never retook Jerusalem. He and Saladin, who never met, agreed a truce in 1192 that opened the holy places to pilgrims.

cards.headline: Richard the Lionheart and Saladin are history’s famous rivals. They never met.
cards.body: They fought each other’s armies and bargained through envoys, but never stood face to face. Here’s the Third Crusade without the legend.

cards.headline: Three rulers answer Hattin
cards.body: Saladin’s victory at Hattin set off the Third Crusade, from 1189 to 1192. The German emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing a river in 1190. Philip II of France and Richard I of England pressed on; on the way, Richard conquered Cyprus, which became a vital supply base. The crusaders took Acre in July 1191. The next month Philip went home, and Richard was left to lead.

cards.headline: Acre’s prisoners
cards.body: Acre shows the side of the Lionheart the legends leave out. Saladin had agreed to pay a ransom for the city’s Muslim garrison. When he failed to pay, Richard had all 2,700 prisoners executed in view of Saladin’s army. Remember the Templars killed after Hattin? Neither leader was above killing prisoners.

cards.headline: So close to Jerusalem
cards.body: Richard beat Saladin’s army at Arsuf in September 1191. Twice he led his forces to within a few miles of Jerusalem, and twice he pulled back; he never retook the city. All the while he bargained with Saladin and his brother al-Adil, with real mutual respect. In September 1192 they agreed a three-year truce: the coast from Jaffa north stayed Christian, and pilgrims had free access to the holy places.

mascot.line: A legend with the edges left in is still a great story. It’s just a truer one.

cards.headline: A king mostly away
cards.body: Sailing home, Richard was captured by Duke Leopold of Austria and handed to the German emperor, Henry VI. He was freed in 1194 for a ransom of 150,000 marks. Richard was king of England from 1189 to 1199 but spent little time there, and recent historians judge him less kindly than his own age did. A famous soldier; a mostly absent king.
