title: The Knights Templar
objective: After this level you can explain who the Templars were and how they fell.
summary: Founded around 1120 to protect pilgrims, the Templars were fighting monks and bankers. Philip IV had them arrested in 1307 on baseless charges; the pope suppressed them in 1312.

cards.headline: They took vows like monks, fought like knights and lent money to kings.
cards.body: The Knights Templar were one of the strangest creations of the Crusades, and one of the richest. So how did they fall so hard?

cards.headline: Guards for the pilgrim road
cards.body: In late 1119 or early 1120, eight or nine French knights led by Hugh de Payns vowed to protect pilgrims traveling to the Holy Land. King Baldwin II of Jerusalem housed them in the area of the former Temple of Solomon, and that gave them their name: the Templars. Within about ten years, the Church formally approved the order at the Council of Troyes.

cards.headline: Monks with swords
cards.body: Templars swore the vows of monks: poverty, chastity and obedience. But the knights fought, in a white surcoat marked with a red cross. The poverty was personal, not collective. Their military strength made them ideal bankers, to kings as well as to pilgrims. Picture a bank whose vault is guarded by the bankers themselves.

mascot.line: Charges invented, confessions forced. Historians read these trial records very carefully.

cards.headline: The arrests of 1307
cards.body: When Acre fell in 1291, the Templars lost much of their reason for being, while their wealth, lands in Europe and power bred resentment. Philip IV of France was chronically short of money. On 13 October 1307 he had every Templar in France arrested. They were accused of heresy and idol worship, and many confessed under torture. The charges are now recognized as baseless.

cards.headline: The end of the order
cards.body: Pope Clement V suppressed the Templars in 1312 and gave their property to another military order, the Hospitallers. In 1314 the last grand master, Jacques de Molay, was burned. The order that began by guarding pilgrims was destroyed by a Christian king who needed money.

title: The Fourth Crusade
objective: After this level you can explain how crusaders ended up sacking Christian Constantinople.
summary: In debt to Venice, the Fourth Crusade took Christian Zara, then followed an exiled prince to Constantinople, sacked it in April 1204 and ruled it as a Latin empire until 1261.

cards.headline: In 1204 crusaders sacked a Christian city: Constantinople.
cards.body: Nobody set out to do that. A debt, a deal and an exiled prince took them there.

cards.headline: A bill in Venice
cards.body: Pope Innocent III called a new crusade in 1198. The crusaders hired Venice to ship them east for 85,000 marks. But when the army gathered in 1202, only about a third of the expected men turned up, and they couldn’t pay. To settle the debt, in November 1202 they attacked and took Zara (Zadar), a Christian city. Imagine booking a bus for thirty friends when only ten show up. The driver still wants the full fare.

cards.headline: A prince’s offer
cards.body: Then came a tempting offer. An exiled Byzantine prince, Alexius, promised the crusaders a huge payment, the Byzantine church’s submission to Rome and help on crusade, if they would put him on the throne in Constantinople. The fleet turned toward the city.

cards.headline: Over the walls from the water
cards.body: Remember Level 4’s walls, which held against attackers through the early Middle Ages? In 1204 the attack came from the water. On 12 April, men climbed from ships’ masts across catwalks onto the walls. For three days the army pillaged at will, defiling and stealing from the holy places. Justinian’s Hagia Sophia, from Level 5, was looted. The four bronze horses of St Mark’s in Venice were brought from Constantinople at this time.

cards.headline: A Latin empire
cards.body: The crusaders made Baldwin of Flanders emperor of a new Latin empire, and Hagia Sophia became a Roman Catholic cathedral. When Pope Innocent III heard how the crusaders had behaved, he was filled with shame and rebuked them. In 1261 Michael VIII Palaeologus retook a much diminished Constantinople. The Crusades had begun with a call to aid the Christians of the East. This one wrecked their capital.

title: The Reconquista
objective: After this level you can describe the centuries-long Christian conquest of Muslim Spain.
summary: From Covadonga around 718 to Granada in 1492, Christian kingdoms retook Iberia from Muslim rule. It began as politics, turned religious, and the peoples stayed closely bound.

cards.headline: Level 8’s conquest of Spain began in 711. Undoing it took until 1492.
cards.body: Historians call it the Reconquista, the “reconquest”. It was the Crusades’ long western story, and more tangled than its name suggests.

cards.headline: Where it started
cards.body: Remember 711? Muslim forces overran most of the Iberian Peninsula, ending the Visigothic kingdom. The Reconquista was the series of campaigns by which Christian states took that land back. Its traditional starting point is the Battle of Covadonga, around 718, when Christians in Asturias, in northern Spain, first held off Muslim forces. The fight back began within ten years; the finish took nearly eight centuries.

cards.headline: Holy war, or politics?
cards.body: The Reconquista began as political expansion by Christian kingdoms. Popes were backing it by the 11th century, but it became explicitly religious only after Muslim power in Spain had been broken. All along, the Christian and Muslim peoples of Spain were tightly bound together, culturally and economically. Rivals on the battlefield were often neighbors everywhere else.

cards.headline: Granada, 1492
cards.body: After Las Navas de Tolosa, the last serious Muslim threat to Christian dominance was gone. One kingdom held out longest: Granada, home of the Alhambra palace, the last Moorish kingdom in Spain. In January 1492 it fell to Ferdinand and Isabella, the Catholic Monarchs. Nearly 800 years after 711, Muslim rule in Spain was over.

title: What the Crusades Changed
objective: After this level you can explain the Crusades' effects on trade, ideas and relations between faiths.
summary: After Acre fell in 1291, the Crusades left richer Italian trading cities, embittered Greeks, long memories among Jews and Muslims, and less effect on learning than once claimed.

cards.headline: In 1291 the last crusader stronghold on the mainland fell. What had changed?
cards.body: The Mamluks took Acre and destroyed it, along with the castles along the coast. The crusader states were gone. Their effects were not.

cards.headline: Winners at the market
cards.body: The clearest winners were Italian trading cities. They gained quarters in the crusader states, extended their trade with the Muslim world and set up trading posts, some lasting long after 1291. Crusading also expanded trade between Europe and the Muslim world, bringing new goods and tastes to European tables. For armies it was holy war. For merchants it was also a very long business trip.

cards.headline: A wound between Christians
cards.body: The Crusades, above all the Fourth (Level 47), so embittered the Greeks that any real reunion of the Eastern and Western churches was out of the question. The Byzantines had asked the West for help in 1095. By 1204 the West had sacked their capital.

cards.headline: Long memories
cards.body: Memories ran deep on every side. For Jews, the Rhineland massacres of 1096 (Level 42) became a turning point in relations with Christians. Muslim writers of the time called the crusaders Franks and saw them as cruel invaders. The same events looked very different depending on who told the story.

cards.headline: What they probably didn’t do
cards.body: Some changes get credited to the Crusades that likely came another way. Unlike Sicily and Spain (Level 48’s Spain), the crusader states do not seem to have been a route for Arabic science and philosophy to reach the West. That’s one reason historians now see the Crusades as one significant factor in Europe’s development, not its single driving force.

title: The Growth of Towns
objective: After this level you can explain why towns grew after the year 1000.
summary: Once the raids ended, towns revived: Europe’s population nearly doubled from 1000 to 1340, new walled towns appeared, and charters offered freedom after a year and a day.

cards.headline: Stay in some medieval towns for a year and a day, and you could become free.
cards.body: Yet for centuries after Rome, town life in western Europe had almost vanished. Then, after about 1000, the towns came back, and people wanted in. Why?

cards.headline: The quiet centuries end
cards.body: Remember Level 1? In the early Middle Ages, about 500 to 1000, frequent warfare made town life in western Europe virtually disappear. Towns only began to grow steadily again once the raids by Vikings, Magyars and Saracens had stopped. Raiders, it turns out, are terrible for business. First came peace, then came the towns.

cards.headline: More people, more towns
cards.body: Then came the people. Between 1000 and 1340, Europe’s population nearly doubled. In the 10th and 11th centuries new towns were founded and old ones spread out, and once a town felt full, its people usually ringed it with a wall. Picture your own hometown doubling in size: new streets, new neighbours, and a wall to keep it all together.

mascot.line: Imagine a fresh start that came with your new address.

cards.headline: City air brings freedom
cards.body: Growing towns wanted settlers, and they had something to offer. Many became communes: self-governing towns whose citizens swore to help each other, holding a charter from a bishop, count or king. Emperor Henry V, who ruled from 1111 to 1125, wrote the principle “city air brings freedom” into charters for Speyer and Worms. New towns on lords’ lands offered freedom and land to settlers who stayed more than a year and a day.

title: Markets and Fairs
objective: After this level you can describe medieval markets and trade fairs.
summary: English markets met weekly by royal charter; fairs met yearly on saints’ days. The Champagne fairs linked north and south, and piepowder courts gave quick justice.

cards.headline: Medieval England had courts named after dusty feet.
cards.body: They sat right at the fairs, settling traders’ arguments on the spot. To see why anyone needed them, follow the money: first to the weekly market, then to the great fairs.

cards.headline: Market day
cards.body: A medieval market wasn’t open every day. In England it met once a week, on a set day and in a set place, and holding one took a royal charter. Towns, villages and monasteries all won them. From 1200 there was a catch: a new market was allowed only if it didn’t harm the markets nearby. Even medieval kings worried about the shop down the road.

cards.headline: Fair season
cards.body: A fair was bigger and rarer: once a year, usually on a saint’s feast day, lasting from a single day to a week or more. The greatest were the Champagne fairs in France, which rotated among four towns, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, and peaked in the 13th century. Under the count’s protection, merchants swapped northern cloth for spices and dyes from the Mediterranean. North met south in a French field.

cards.headline: Credit and quick justice
cards.body: Big deals needed trust. At the Champagne fairs, bargains often ran on letters of credit rather than bags of coins, laying groundwork for modern credit. And when a deal went wrong in England, a piepowder court (from the French for “dusty feet”) settled disputes at fairs and markets fast and on the spot, before the traveller could dust off and leave.

title: Guilds
objective: After this level you can explain how guilds controlled crafts and trained apprentices.
summary: Craft guilds grew in busy towns, held a monopoly, set quality and prices, and trained members from apprentice to journeyman to master.

cards.headline: A “masterpiece” was once a job application.
cards.body: In a medieval town, you couldn’t just hang out a sign and start making shoes. The trade belonged to a guild, and to join its top rank you had to prove yourself.

cards.headline: Two kinds of guild
cards.body: Merchant guilds brought together a town’s merchants. Craft guilds brought together the artisans of one trade: the bakers, say, or the weavers. Craft guilds arose soon after merchant guilds, in growing towns where work was splitting into many specialised trades. Once a town needed a baker, a butcher and a candlestick maker, it needed rules for all of them.

cards.headline: Rules of the trade
cards.body: A craft guild held a monopoly on its trade in town: if you weren’t in the guild, you didn’t sell. It set standards for the quality of goods and worked to keep prices stable. It also looked after its own, with a patron saint, a chapel in the parish church, charitable work and often a guildhall. Part quality inspector, part trade association, part social club.

mascot.line: Five to nine years of training. Suddenly a driving test looks quick.

cards.headline: Apprentice, journeyman, master
cards.body: Guild members climbed a ladder. An apprentice, usually a boy in late childhood or his teens, lived with the master’s family for a fixed term of five to nine years. Then he became a journeyman: the “journey” originally meant a day’s labour, and journeymen worked for wages, often by the day. To rise to master, a journeyman might have to prove his skill with a masterpiece.

title: Food and Feasts
objective: After this level you can describe what rich and poor people ate.
summary: Bread, meat and drink marked rank: white wheat for lords and coarse loaves for servants, meat rarely for peasants, fish on fast days. Spices were costly status symbols, not a cover for rotten meat.

cards.headline: A medieval dinner could tell you exactly who was sitting at the table.
cards.body: Not by name cards, but by the bread, the meat and the pepper. Let’s eat our way up the social ladder.

cards.headline: Your bread is your rank
cards.body: In a castle kitchen, the baker made fine white wheat rolls for the lady’s table and rough loaves of barley, oats or even peas and beans for the servants. At a feast, food was often served on a slice of bread that soaked up the juices, and you ate with your fingers: forks did not appear on medieval tables. Your plate could be dinner too.

cards.headline: Meat means money
cards.body: Meat on the table was a sign of status. Peasants ate it only rarely, mostly before winter, when livestock was culled so that fewer animals had to be fed through the cold months. Religious fasting banned meat on Fridays and many other days, so fish took its place. At a feast, lower-ranking guests got coarser bread and second-quality ale; wine was expensive, because it had to be imported.

mascot.line: Myth spotted: the rotten-meat story falls apart once you check the price of pepper.

cards.headline: Pepper for show
cards.body: Spices were costly imports, and lords served strong-tasting sauces with expensive foreign spices to show off their wealth. You may have heard that spices hid the taste of rotten meat. Historians reject that: spices cost far more than fresh meat, and salting and smoking preserved food better. Spices weren’t a cover-up. They were a boast.

title: Clothes and Status
objective: After this level you can describe medieval clothes and what they said about status.
summary: Wool clothed almost everyone, from cheap russet to costly scarlet. England’s 1363 law set what each rank could wear, and a 1463 law capped pointed shoes, whose fashion shows up in medieval bones.

cards.headline: Your medieval neighbours could read your rank from across the street.
cards.body: No ID card needed: the cloth on your back did the talking. It talked so loudly that the law stepped in.

cards.headline: Wool for everyone, but not the same wool
cards.body: In 14th-century England, wool was the fabric people bought most, and linen came second. But “wool” covered a huge range, from cheap, coarse russet and blanket to costly scarlet. Two people could both wear wool and still look worlds apart, the way a cheap T-shirt and a designer one are both cotton.

cards.headline: Dressing by law
cards.body: In 1363 England passed a law setting what cloth each rank could wear, from servants and craftsmen up to merchants and knights. It blamed the “outrageous and excessive apparel” of people dressing above their “estate and degree”. The lowest ranks were limited to blanket and russet worth no more than 12 pence. Did it work? Laws like this have proved difficult or impossible to enforce over the long term.

mascot.line: Fashion leaves clues: sometimes in the wardrobe, sometimes in the skeleton.

cards.headline: The pointy-shoe problem
cards.body: Late-medieval fashion loved poulaines, shoes with long pointed toes. In 1463 King Edward IV limited the points in London to under two inches. The fashion left marks you can still measure: Cambridge researchers found bunions in 6% of people buried in the 11th to 13th centuries, but 27% of those buried in the 14th and 15th. The bones kept the receipts.

title: Windmills and Watermills
objective: After this level you can explain how mills changed medieval work.
summary: England had thousands of watermills by 1086, and windmills from the 1180s. Lords claimed the right to grind their tenants’ grain, so Abbot Samson destroyed a rival mill.

cards.headline: In 1191 an abbot ordered a brand-new windmill torn down.
cards.body: Its builder, Herbert the dean, hadn’t asked permission. Why wreck a perfectly good machine? Because in the Middle Ages a mill meant power, in both senses.

cards.headline: Rivers at work
cards.body: Water came first. In 1086 a royal survey counted more than 5,000 water mills in England south of the rivers Severn and Trent. Their wheels ground grain into flour. Later, waterwheels would also drive saws, bellows for forges, trip-hammers and textile mills. For a medieval village, the river was the power socket.

cards.headline: Then the wind
cards.body: Windmills weren’t a European invention: the earliest-known references come from Persia, in 644 and 915. In England, the first written references that clearly mention windmills date from the 1180s. These were timber post mills: the whole body, millstones, gears and all, turned on one great post to face the wind. Imagine turning a wooden shed to catch the breeze.

cards.headline: The lord’s mill
cards.body: A lord could claim soke, or suit of mill: the right to grind all the grain used on his manor at his mill. The miller took his pay as a toll, a share of each person’s grain. So Abbot Samson saw the dean’s windmill as competition: the town’s burgesses would take their grain there instead. “I give you as many thanks as if you had cut off both my feet,” he told the dean. The frightened dean pulled it down himself.

title: Medicine and the Four Humors
objective: After this level you can explain medieval ideas about health and healing.
summary: Medieval medicine sought balance among four humours. Physicians read urine and let blood to remove an excess; bloodletting was later discredited.

cards.headline: A medieval physician might hold your urine up to the light and study it.
cards.body: He was hunting for clues about four liquids that, he believed, ran your whole body: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Welcome to the four humours.

cards.headline: Four liquids in balance
cards.body: The theory was ancient. Hippocrates championed it, and Galen, Rome’s leading medical authority in the 2nd century CE, built on it; it was still current throughout the Middle Ages. The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler) and black bile (melancholy). The ideal person had them perfectly balanced, and illness meant one had got out of proportion. Health was a recipe, and sickness meant too much of one ingredient.

cards.headline: Reading the signs
cards.body: So how do you spot an imbalance you can’t see? Medieval physicians examined a patient’s urine: its colour, its consistency, its clarity and any sediment, all read as signs of the humours inside. A flask held up to the window was the medieval version of a lab test.

cards.headline: Letting out the excess
cards.body: If one humour was in excess, healers tried to remove it, by letting blood or applying leeches. After a church edict of 1163 barred clergy from bloodletting, barber-surgeons took it up alongside shaving and pulling teeth, a legacy you can still see in the barber’s pole. Bloodletting lost credibility in the 18th and 19th centuries, when studies showed it worked less well than claimed.
cards.callout: This is the history of an idea, not medical advice

mascot.line: Next time someone seems melancholic, remember: a medieval doctor would have blamed black bile.

cards.headline: Words that outlived the theory
cards.body: A person ruled by one humour was called sanguine (from the Latin for blood), phlegmatic, choleric or melancholic. The theory is long discredited, but the words stayed in English. To a medieval doctor, a sanguine friend was simply someone with plenty of blood.

title: Women in the Middle Ages
objective: After this level you can describe the lives, work and power of medieval women.
summary: By class and region: Christine de Pizan wrote for a living, Margaret Paston ran estates, brewsters and Paris silkwomen worked in trade, and coverture limited wives.

cards.headline: In 1405 a French widow built a city out of words.
cards.body: Its citizens were famous women, and its author, Christine de Pizan, is a good guide to what medieval women could do, and what they couldn’t.

cards.headline: Living by the pen
cards.body: Christine de Pizan (1364 to about 1430) was widowed after ten years of marriage, with three children to raise. She took up writing to support them. In The Book of the City of Ladies (1405) she wrote of women known for heroism and virtue, and she defended women against misogynist satire. She argued back, in print, and it paid the bills.

cards.headline: Running the estate
cards.body: In England, the gentry had their own formidable women. Margaret Paston (about 1421 to 1484) was a Norfolk gentlewoman. She left the largest collection of personal letters from medieval England, many to her husband while he was away. While he was away she managed the family’s estates, and when attackers threatened their manor house she defended it and asked him for crossbows and armour.

cards.headline: Women at work
cards.body: In towns and villages, women worked for money. Women brewed and sold most of the ale drunk in medieval England; after 1350, men slowly took over the trade. In 13th- and 14th-century Paris, the silk industry even had some all-female guilds, and a few silkwomen did business with aristocrats and the king himself.

cards.headline: The legal limits
cards.body: The law set hard limits too. Under English coverture, rooted in Norman custom, a wife’s legal existence was suspended: she could not make contracts or sue in her own name, though a single woman could. So what a medieval woman could do depended heavily on her class, her region and whether she was married.

title: Songs, Games and Holidays
objective: After this level you can describe how medieval people spent their free time.
summary: "Holiday" means holy day. York’s guilds staged 48 plays on Corpus Christi, villages played football despite royal bans, and songs like "Sumer is icumen in" survive.

cards.headline: In 1314 England’s king banned football. It didn’t work.
cards.body: Medieval people worked hard, but they played hard too. So when did they get time off, and what did they do with it?

cards.headline: Holy days
cards.body: Free time followed the Church calendar. The word holiday comes from Old English haligdæg, “holy day”: a day set apart for religious observance. By the 14th century a holiday could also mean a day off work. Your summer holiday is, word for word, a holy day.

cards.headline: The whole town on stage
cards.body: On the summer feast of Corpus Christi, York put on a show. Its craft guilds performed a cycle of 48 plays, from the 14th century on, rolling them through the streets on pageant wagons. Each guild took a scene, sometimes one that suited its trade: the Shipwrights performed the Building of the Ark. Typecasting, medieval style.

mascot.line: Five royal bans in about a century, and the ball kept rolling.

cards.headline: Football with no rulebook
cards.body: Folk football was usually played at Shrovetide or Easter, village against village, across fields, through streams and down narrow streets. Everyone joined in: men and women, rich and poor, clergy too. Edward II banned it in 1314, and later kings banned it again in 1349, 1389, 1401 and 1423. All in vain. The game kept winning.

cards.headline: Sing, cuckoo
cards.body: Songs survive too. “Sumer is icumen in”, a round with the refrain “sing cuckoo”, was written down at Reading Abbey in the mid-13th century, and the manuscript is now in the British Library. A song about summer arriving, still singable after more than seven centuries.

title: The House of Wisdom
objective: After this level you can explain how Baghdad became a center of learning.
summary: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750; al-Mansur founded Baghdad as the Round City in 762. Al-Ma'mun sponsored Greek translation; the House of Wisdom's scope is debated.

cards.headline: In 762 a caliph built his capital as a circle. It became a city of translators.
cards.body: Under the caliph al-Ma’mun, Baghdad turned ancient Greek books into Arabic. At the heart of the story sits a famous name, the House of Wisdom. What was it, really?

cards.headline: A new family, a round city
cards.body: Remember Level 8’s Umayyad caliphs, ruling from Damascus? In 750 a new family, the Abbasids, overthrew them, and the capital later moved to a brand-new city. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur chose the site of Baghdad and built Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace, inside circular walls. Everyone called it the Round City. Most capitals grow; this one was drawn.

cards.headline: Greek books, Arabic words
cards.body: The caliph al-Ma’mun, who reigned from 813 to 833, encouraged the translation of ancient Greek works into Arabic. From about 800 to 1000, a large-scale translation movement carried Aristotle, Euclid and much more into Arabic. Picture a whole library learning a new language, one book at a time.

mascot.line: A famous building that might have been mostly a bookshelf. History loves a plot twist.

cards.headline: The House of Wisdom puzzle

It is often pictured as a great academy at the centre of everything. Historians are more careful: little evidence puts it at the centre of Baghdad’s scholarship, so its scope is debated. The translating itself is not in doubt. The legend may be bigger than the building; the books were real.

title: Algebra and Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain how al-Khwarizmi and others shaped mathematics.
summary: Al-Khwarizmi's al-jabr book named algebra and his Latin name gave us algorithm. The numerals came from India, through the Islamic world, to Europe.

cards.headline: Say “algorithm” and you’re saying a Baghdad scholar’s name.
cards.body: Say “algebra” and you’re quoting the title of his book. Meet al-Khwarizmi, and the numbers he helped carry west.

cards.headline: A book about balancing
cards.body: Al-Khwarizmi, who lived from about 780 to 850, worked at the House of Wisdom you met in Level 61. Around 825 he wrote a book on calculating by al-jabr and balancing. Al-jabr, “restoring”, meant moving a subtracted term to the other side of an equation; balancing cancelled what matched on both sides. Its Latin translation in the 12th century gave us the word algebra. If you’ve ever moved x to the other side, you’ve done al-jabr.

cards.headline: Numbers from India
cards.body: The digits you use every day originated in India in the 6th or 7th century. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book of arithmetic with them, which survives in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, “Al-Khwarizmi Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning”. That Latin spelling of his name, Algoritmi, became our word algorithm. Hence “Hindu-Arabic” numerals: invented in India, carried by the Islamic world.

cards.headline: Into Europe
cards.body: Mathematicians of the Islamic world, especially al-Khwarizmi and al-Kindi, brought the numerals to Europe about the 12th century. Even so, when Fibonacci published his Liber abaci in 1202, few Europeans knew them. He had learned calculation from an Arab master in North Africa, and his book spread the system. Next time you do long division, thank a chain of scholars from India to Pisa.

title: Astronomy and the Astrolabe
objective: After this level you can explain how Islamic scholars studied the sky with astrolabes.
summary: The Greek astrolabe reached the Islamic world by the 8th century, found prayer times and the qibla, and was refined (al-Zarqali). Many star names come from Arabic.

cards.headline: Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Vega, Altair: the night sky speaks Arabic.
cards.body: Look up tonight and you’re reading names adopted from Arabic. Behind them is a brass instrument that helped find the direction of Mecca and the five daily prayer times.

cards.headline: A Greek star-taker
cards.body: The astrolabe’s name is Greek, roughly “star-taker”, and it probably began around the time of the astronomer Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE. A star map called the rete turned over a plate made for one latitude, and a sighting rule measured a star’s height to find the time. The astrolabe reached the Islamic world by the 8th century. Borrowed, yes. Left alone, no.

cards.headline: Refined for prayer and for everywhere
cards.body: In the Islamic world, astrolabes found the qibla, the direction of Mecca, and the five daily prayer times. Astronomers kept refining the design. In Toledo, al-Zarqali (1029–1100) made a universal astrolabe that needed no separate plate for each latitude, and as the Saphea Arzachelis it was widely used in medieval Europe. One instrument for every city: that’s an upgrade.
cards.callout: Invented by Greeks, refined in the Islamic world

mascot.line: Next clear night, find Aldebaran trailing the Pleiades. It has been following them for a very long time.

cards.headline: Names in the sky
cards.body: Arab astronomers also translated the star descriptions of Ptolemy’s Almagest, a Greek catalog from around 150 CE. In the 10th century the Persian astronomer al-Sufi updated it with his own catalog, later translated into European languages. That’s how Aldebaran got its name: “the follower”, because it follows the Pleiades across the sky. Stargazers everywhere are quietly speaking Arabic.

summary: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, translated into Latin in the 12th century, was a European textbook until the mid-1600s. Bimaristans admitted all; Qalawun's hospital was free.

cards.headline: Europe’s doctors were still learning from a Persian’s textbook in the 1600s.
cards.body: It was written in Arabic, far from any European classroom. How did it get onto their reading lists? And what did hospitals look like where it was written?

cards.headline: The boy who found medicine easy
cards.body: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara in 980 and died in Hamadan in 1037. He turned to medicine at 16 and, by his own account, found it “easy”. (Most of us found algebra hard at 16.) His great work, the Canon of Medicine, runs to five books, from general principles and simple drugs to diseases and compound remedies.

cards.headline: Europe’s textbook
cards.body: In the 12th century Gerard of Cremona translated the Canon into Latin. Between 1500 and 1674 some sixty editions were published in Europe, mostly for university medical training, and it served as a textbook there until the mid-17th century. Imagine a course reading list that stays the same for centuries.
cards.callout: Written in Arabic, taught in Latin

mascot.line: Free care, separate wards, open to all. Some ideas age very well.

cards.headline: Hospitals for everyone
cards.body: The Islamic world built hospitals called bimaristans, a Persian word meaning “location of disease”. Harun al-Rashid founded one in Baghdad, and al-Ma’mun founded more. Hospitals at Baghdad, Damascus and Córdoba admitted patients regardless of religion, race or social rank. In Cairo, Sultan Qalawun’s hospital of 1284–85 treated rich and poor free of charge, with separate wards for different illnesses. No insurance card required.

title: Paper and Books
objective: After this level you can explain how papermaking spread from China through the Islamic world.
summary: Paper began in China as medicine wrapping. Papermaking reached Samarkand in 751 (the Talas story is legend), Baghdad by the 790s and Europe by the 12th century.

cards.headline: Paper’s first job wasn’t writing. It was wrapping medicine.
cards.body: Chinese craftsmen made it from washed rags. The trip from China to Baghdad took centuries, and it comes with a famous legend attached.

cards.headline: Made in China
cards.body: Chinese craftsmen first made paper by washing rags and drying them on a screen. Its first use, in the 2nd century BCE, was packaging medicine. Within a century it began to replace bamboo strips for writing, and by the 3rd and 4th centuries CE the Chinese wrote everything on it. From pill wrapper to page: not a bad career.

cards.headline: The Talas legend
cards.body: Chinese paper travelled along the Silk Road into Central Asia before the craft of making it did. Before 712, a ruler near Samarkand wrote on imported sheets, reusing ones already written on one side. Papermaking itself reached Samarkand in 751. Legend says Chinese craftsmen captured at the Battle of Talas that year taught their captors the secret. Most scholars think the craft moved west earlier.
cards.callout: The Talas prisoners are a traditional story, not settled history

cards.headline: Baghdad’s paper, Europe’s turn
cards.body: Paper was being made in Baghdad by the 790s, under the caliph Harun al-Rashid, and soon scholars across the Islamic world were copying manuscripts onto it. Remember Level 7’s monks, writing on parchment or vellum made from animal skin? Paper came from rags instead. It reached Europe through Sicily and Spain by the 12th century. Old shirts in, libraries out.

title: Tang and Song China
objective: After this level you can describe inventions of medieval China, from printing to gunpowder.

cards.headline: Printing, gunpowder, the compass: a famous thinker said they changed the world.
cards.body: The English philosopher Francis Bacon never realized that all three came from China. Meet the two dynasties behind them: the Tang (618–907) and the Song (960–1279).

cards.headline: Printing, one block at a time
cards.body: Printing was invented under the Tang, first to spread Buddhist scriptures and later calendars and dictionaries. Printers carved a whole page of text into a single wooden block. The Diamond Sutra, printed in 868, is the first known dated printed book. Around 1041–48 Bi Sheng went further, with movable type of baked clay, though China didn’t follow it up. One block per page is slow; one piece per character is clever.

cards.headline: Sparks and a needle
cards.body: Gunpowder, a mix of saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal, originated in China, where people used it in fireworks and signals by the 10th century. Under the Song, advances in compasses, charts and instruments helped ships trade over long distances. Its first big jobs were lighting up the sky and finding the way across the sea.

mascot.line: From pill wrapper to banknote. Paper had a very good few centuries.

cards.headline: Money made of paper
cards.body: The Song pioneered paper money as legal tender, which helped a booming commercial economy. Several Song cities had populations of more than 1,000,000. Remember Level 65, where paper started out wrapping medicine? Under the Song it had become money itself. Quite a promotion.

title: Genghis Khan and the Mongols
objective: After this level you can explain how the Mongols built the largest land empire in history.
summary: Temujin became Genghis Khan in 1206; his heirs built the largest contiguous land empire. Death tolls are rough but vast. In 1258 Hulegu sacked Baghdad.

cards.headline: In 1206 a Mongol leader took a new name. His empire grew to 23 million sq km.
cards.body: Chinggis Khan, whom we call Genghis, founded the largest land empire in one piece the world has seen. The price, in lives, was staggering.

cards.headline: From Temujin to Genghis Khan
cards.body: Temujin was born around 1162. In 1206 an assembly of Mongol leaders declared him universal ruler, Chinggis Khan. He died in 1227, and the empire kept growing. At its peak it ran from the Pacific to the Danube, some 23 million sq km: the largest contiguous land empire in history. No empire in one piece has been bigger since.

cards.headline: Counting the dead
cards.body: No one kept reliable totals, and medieval chroniclers exaggerated. Even so, the numbers are vast. Britannica estimates that Genghis Khan’s conquests killed roughly 40 million people, especially in China and what is now Iran. For China, one estimate has the population falling from about 100 million to 65 million, mostly because livelihoods were destroyed rather than by direct killing. Allowing for exaggeration, nothing before had devastated Muslim Asia like it.
cards.callout: Estimates vary widely; every one of them is enormous

cards.headline: Baghdad, 1258
cards.body: Remember Level 61’s Round City? In 1258 Genghis Khan’s grandson Hulegu sacked Baghdad, killed the caliph and massacred hundreds of thousands of its people. The Abbasid dynasty fell. Whatever remained of the House of Wisdom’s collection was destroyed. Nearly five centuries of a capital, broken in one campaign.

title: The Silk Road
objective: After this level you can explain how the Silk Road linked China, Persia and Europe.
summary: The Silk Road was a 6,400 km network worked in stages by middlemen, carrying goods and religions. The Pax Mongolica made its routes safer in the 13th and 14th centuries.

cards.headline: Almost nobody travelled the whole Silk Road. That’s how it worked.
cards.body: It ran about 6,400 km, yet goods crossed it in stages, handled by middleman after middleman. Then the Mongols changed the rules of the road.

cards.headline: A relay, not a road
cards.body: The Silk Road was a network of routes, about 6,400 km long, linking China with the Mediterranean. Few people travelled all of it; goods were handled in stages by middlemen. Silk went west, while wool, gold and silver went east. Think of a relay race where the baton was a bale of silk.

cards.headline: Ideas in the luggage
cards.body: Beliefs travelled too. Buddhism, from India, reached China along the Silk Road, and so did Nestorian Christianity. Remember Level 65’s paper? Chinese sheets moved along these routes into Central Asia before the craft of making them did. The goods were silk; the passengers were ideas.

cards.headline: The Mongol peace
cards.body: In the 13th and 14th centuries the Silk Road revived under the Mongols. Historians call it the Pax Mongolica, a time of relative stability, trade and exchange. Despite the violence of the conquests, merchants, diplomats and scholars could cross Mongol lands with unprecedented security. The Mongols expanded the yam, a network of postal and supply stations, and merchants carrying paiza passes had imperial protection. The same empire that wrecked cities guarded the roads between them.

title: Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta
objective: After this level you can compare two great medieval travelers.
summary: Marco Polo dictated his Travels to Rustichello; parts are exaggerated, but evidence shows he was in China. Ibn Battuta left Tangier in 1325 and travelled some 120,000 km.

cards.headline: Two great medieval travellers. Two famous books. Two ghostwriters.
cards.body: Marco Polo reached Kublai Khan’s China; Ibn Battuta wandered even farther. Both told their stories to a writer who added polish, and both journeys were eased by Level 68’s Mongol peace. So how much can we trust them?

cards.headline: Marco Polo’s China
cards.body: Marco Polo, born in Venice about 1254, set out for Asia in 1271, aged 17 or 18, with his father and uncle. They reached Kublai Khan’s court about 1275, and Marco stayed in Asia until 1295, 17 of those years in China. Captured in 1298 in a war between Venice and Genoa, he dictated his story in captivity to Rustichello of Pisa, a writer of romances. A travel memoir co-written by a novelist: what could go wrong?

cards.headline: Did he really go?
cards.body: Parts are debated. Polo claimed Hangzhou had 12,000 bridges; a later traveller found only 347, suburbs included. In the 1990s the historian Frances Wood argued he may never have reached China, since he never mentions the Great Wall, tea or foot-binding. But in 2012 Hans Ulrich Vogel showed that Polo’s details of Chinese money, salt and revenues closely match Chinese sources. He was there. He just rounded up.

cards.headline: Ibn Battuta’s world
cards.body: Ibn Battuta was born in Tangier, Morocco, in 1304. In 1325, at 21, he set out on the hajj to Mecca and resolved never to travel any road a second time. He served for years as a judge in Delhi, and in 1342 the sultan made him his envoy to China. His wanderings covered some 120,000 km, hardly surpassed before the age of steam. Back home he dictated his Rihla to Ibn Juzayy, who embellished the prose.

title: Magna Carta
objective: After this level you can explain what Magna Carta said in 1215 and why it still matters.
summary: In June 1215 rebel barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta. The Pope annulled it within ten weeks, but it was reissued in 1216, 1217 and 1225, and three clauses are still law.

cards.headline: In June 1215 a king agreed to a charter. By August, the Pope had killed it.
cards.body: Magna Carta, the “Great Charter”, was dead in less than ten weeks. So why does anyone still care about it? Because it refused to stay dead.

cards.headline: Peace terms in a meadow
cards.body: By 1215 England’s barons had had enough of King John. The rebels renounced their allegiance and occupied London. On 15 June, at Runnymede, a meadow between Windsor and Staines, John agreed to their charter. Its most famous promise, clause 39: no free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by the lawful judgment of his equals or the law of the land. Clause 40 added that the king would not sell, deny or delay justice to anyone. In short: the king can’t just lock you up.

mascot.line: Ten weeks from peace deal to scrap paper. Hold that thought: this charter has a very long second act.

cards.headline: Dead in ten weeks
cards.body: It didn’t last. John had submitted his kingdom to the Pope, so he appealed to him. On 24 August 1215, less than ten weeks after Runnymede, Pope Innocent III annulled the charter, calling it “shameful, demeaning, illegal and unjust”. Fighting broke out again in September and went on until John died in October 1216. As peace deals go, it was a flop.

cards.headline: The charter that kept coming back
cards.body: Then something odd happened. After John’s death the charter was reissued in the name of his young son, Henry III, in 1216 and again in 1217. In 1225 it came back once more, this time in exchange for a new tax. The failed peace deal had become a bargain: rights for money. And pieces of it are still here. Three clauses remain in English law today: the freedom of the English Church, the ancient liberties of the City of London, and the right to lawful judgment.

title: The First Parliaments
objective: After this level you can explain how parliaments began in England and elsewhere.
summary: Kings needed consent for extra taxes, so councils grew into parliaments: León in 1188, the word in England by 1236, towns summoned in 1265, the Model Parliament of 1295 and a separate Commons in 1341.

cards.headline: Parliament began as a conversation. Its root is French parler, “to speak”.
cards.body: Kings didn’t set up parliaments out of kindness. They needed something only their subjects could hand over, and asking was the price.

cards.headline: A council gets a name
cards.body: In England the word parliament first turns up in 1236, for the king’s Great Council of great men. England wasn’t first, though. In 1188 the Spanish kingdom of León held an assembly where elected representatives of the towns sat with the king, the church and the nobles. UNESCO calls its decrees the oldest documentary evidence of Europe’s parliamentary system. Parliaments weren’t one country’s bright idea.

cards.headline: Money talks
cards.body: Here’s why they caught on. Wars cost more than a king could pay from his own wealth. Edward I and the kings after him needed extra taxes, and they needed Parliament’s agreement to raise them. Remember Level 71? Magna Carta itself had been reissued in 1225 in exchange for a new tax. Ask people for money often enough, and they start asking for things back.
cards.callout: No consent, no extra tax

mascot.line: Two knights from every county, two burgesses from every town. The House of Commons started as a very long guest list.

cards.headline: Who got a seat
cards.body: In 1265 Simon de Montfort, rebelling against Henry III, summoned a parliament that for the first time included representatives of both counties and towns. Edward I’s Model Parliament of 1295 made it the pattern: nobles and bishops, plus two knights from each county and two burgesses from each town. In 1341 the knights and burgesses met separately for the first time, forming what became the House of Commons. Two rooms, and the start of two houses.

title: Common Law and Juries
objective: After this level you can explain how common law and trial by jury developed.
summary: Under Henry II the king's courts built a common law for all England. His Assize of Clarendon (1166) created juries that named suspects; after 1215 juries also decided guilt.

cards.headline: The first English juries didn’t decide who was guilty. They named suspects.
cards.body: Under Henry II, twelve local men were the king’s informers. How did a jury go from pointing fingers to deciding cases? The answer runs through 1215.

cards.headline: One law for all England
cards.body: Henry II, king from 1154 to 1189, sent royal officials around the country to look into how justice was being done. Out of the king’s courts grew common law: law common to all England, instead of a patchwork of local customs. Judges came to follow earlier decisions as precedent, so each ruling guided the next. Think of a family recipe book: nobody wrote it in one go, but every cook adds a page.

cards.headline: Twelve men of the hundred
cards.body: In 1166 Henry’s Assize of Clarendon told each hundred, a district of a county, to pick 12 men (and each township 4) to report crimes and name suspects to the king’s travelling judges. This jury decided who should be accused, not who was guilty. It was the ancestor of today’s grand jury. Picture a neighbourhood watch with the king’s judges on speed dial.

mascot.line: Same twelve neighbours, new job: from naming suspects to deciding verdicts.

cards.headline: From accusers to deciders
cards.body: Then, in 1215, the Church pulled its priests out of trials by ordeal (Level 74 has the gory details). England needed a new way to settle guilt, and it had a group of sworn neighbours ready: the jury. Soon juries were deciding guilt as well. On the continent, Level 5’s Justinian code became the root of civil law. England went its own way, and its common law later spread to the United States and most of the Commonwealth.

title: Trial by Ordeal
objective: After this level you can explain trial by ordeal and trial by combat.
summary: Ordeals of hot iron and cold water, and trial by combat, asked God to reveal the truth. The Church's 1215 ban ended ordeals in England; trial by battle lasted until 1819.

cards.headline: Guilty or innocent? In medieval England, a pond might decide.
cards.body: Before juries weighed evidence, a court could hand the question to God. The tests were brutal, but they had their own strict logic.

cards.headline: Let God decide
cards.body: An ordeal was a physical test, based on the belief that the result would show God’s judgment. Fire and water were the favourites. In the ordeal of hot iron, the accused held a red-hot iron. The hand was bandaged and checked three days later: a clean, healing wound meant innocent; an infected one meant guilty. Your verdict depended on your skin.

mascot.line: Winning by sinking. Medieval justice had some very unusual scoring rules.

cards.headline: Sink to win
cards.body: The cold-water ordeal ran the other way from what you’d expect. The accused went into the water. Sinking meant innocent, because the water had accepted you. Floating meant guilty: the water had rejected you. So the good result was the one where somebody had to fish you out.

cards.headline: Trial by combat
cards.body: After the Norman Conquest, England had another option: trial by combat. The two sides, or champions fighting for them, battled it out on the belief that God would give victory to whoever was in the right. Women, children, clergy and the old or infirm could name a champion. It lingered for centuries: a defendant claimed it in 1818, and Parliament abolished it in 1819.

cards.headline: The end of the ordeal
cards.body: An ordeal needed a priest to bless the iron or the water. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade that blessing, and in England the ordeal soon came to an end. Remember Level 73? The jury stepped in to decide guilt. Without God’s test, people had to weigh the evidence themselves.

title: The Hundred Years' War
objective: After this level you can explain why England and France fought on and off for over a century.
summary: From 1337 to 1453 England and France fought on and off over Edward III's claim to the French crown and England's lands in Gascony. England ended with only Calais.

cards.headline: The Hundred Years’ War lasted 116 years. And nobody at the time called it that.
cards.body: The name came later, from historians. What people lived through was a long, stop-start fight between England and France. So what were they fighting about?

cards.headline: A crown claimed through a mother
cards.body: In 1328 King Charles IV of France died without a son. His nephew, Edward III of England, claimed the French throne through his mother, Isabella, Charles’s sister. The French chose Philip of Valois instead. Imagine a relative inheriting the family house because everyone agreed to skip your mother’s side. Edward did not let it go.

cards.headline: A king who was also a vassal
cards.body: There was an older sore, too. England’s kings held Gascony, in southwest France, as vassals of the French king. That gave the king of France frequent excuses to interfere there. So the king of England was also, in Gascony, a lord answering to Paris. That arrangement was never going to be comfortable.

cards.headline: On and off, for 116 years
cards.body: Fighting started in 1337 and ended in 1453, broken by long truces: less one war than a string of them. And the result? title: Crécy and Agincourt
objective: After this level you can explain how English longbows won at Crécy and Agincourt.
summary: At Crécy (1346) longbows outshot crossbows and broke repeated charges; at Agincourt (1415) archers behind stakes beat the French across a muddy field. Army sizes are debated.

cards.headline: Two famous English wins. The bows are certain. The head counts are not.
cards.body: At Crécy and Agincourt, English archers beat bigger French armies during the Hundred Years’ War. How much bigger? Historians still argue, so you’ll get ranges, not a single number.

cards.headline: Crécy, 1346
cards.body: On 26 August 1346, Edward III’s army met the French at Crécy. Italian crossbowmen opened the French attack and were routed by English archers, whose longbows could shoot about three times as fast. Then came the French charges, some 15 or 16 of them, each cut down by arrows. Three arrows for every bolt is a hard trade to win.

mascot.line: Mud, stakes and a narrow field: sometimes the ground picks the winner before anyone draws a bow.

cards.headline: Agincourt, 1415
cards.body: On 25 October 1415, Henry V’s army stood on a recently ploughed field squeezed between woods. The archers had driven sharpened stakes into the ground in front of them. The French had to advance through mud, straight into the arrows. The battle probably lasted no more than three hours. The field did half the fighting.

cards.headline: Counting with the paperwork
cards.body: How do you count an army centuries later? Historian Anne Curry worked through the muster rolls and financial records, the payroll of the Agincourt campaign. She argues the vast French army once claimed couldn’t even have fitted on the battlefield. Still outnumbered, then, but not hopelessly: a hard win built on arrows and mud.

title: Joan of Arc
objective: After this level you can explain Joan of Arc's rise, trial and legacy.
summary: Joan of Arc helped lift the siege of Orléans and saw Charles VII crowned in 1429. Captured in 1430, she was tried at Rouen, burned in 1431, cleared in 1456 and made a saint in 1920.

cards.headline: A farmer’s daughter turned the war around. Then a court set a trap for her.
cards.body: We know what Joan of Arc said at her trial, because the record survives. First, how she got there.

cards.headline: Voices and a siege
cards.body: Joan was born about 1412, the daughter of a tenant farmer at Domrémy in eastern France. She believed the voices of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret were telling her to help the dauphin Charles and drive out the English. In May 1429 she helped lift the English siege of Orléans. On 17 July Charles was crowned at Reims, with Joan near the altar holding her banner. From a siege to a coronation in about ten weeks.

cards.headline: Captured and tried
cards.body: In 1430 Burgundian troops, allies of the English, captured her at Compiègne and handed her over to the English. From January 1431 a church court at Rouen, led by Pierre Cauchon, Bishop of Beauvais, put her on trial. Its record is unusually full for a medieval trial, so we can still read the judges’ questions and her answers.

mascot.line: No yes, no no, and no way to catch her. The record kept her exact words.

cards.headline: The trick question
cards.body: The judges asked whether she knew she was in God’s grace. It was a trap: the Church held that no one could know. Say yes, and she sounded like a heretic; say no, and she admitted guilt. On 24 February 1431 Joan answered: “If I am not, may God place me there; if I am, may God so keep me.” Neither yes nor no, and nothing to catch.

cards.headline: Condemned, then cleared
cards.body: The court condemned her anyway. After recanting in May, she was found wearing men’s clothes again and declared a relapsed heretic. On 30 May 1431 she was burned at the stake in Rouen, aged about 19. In 1455–56 a retrial authorised by Pope Callixtus III annulled her sentence, and in 1920 she was made a saint.

title: Robin Hood and King Arthur
objective: After this level you can explain how medieval legends like Robin Hood and King Arthur grew.
summary: Robin Hood and King Arthur are legends, not proven history. Robin first appears in rhymes around 1377; Arthur in the Historia Brittonum around 830. Each retelling added more.

cards.headline: Two of the most famous medieval heroes may never have lived. Their stories did.
cards.body: Nobody has proved Robin Hood or King Arthur were real people. What we can trace is how their stories grew, one retelling at a time.

cards.headline: Robin: from rhymes to ballads
cards.body: Robin first appears in writing around 1377, in the poem Piers Plowman: a lazy priest doesn’t know his prayers properly, but he does know “rhymes of Robin Hood”. So the tales were already popular. The oldest surviving ballad, Robin Hood and the Monk, dates from about 1450. Whether a real man stood behind them, no one has shown. He may only ever have been a legend.

mascot.line: No Marian in the oldest ballads! Legends collect characters like a snowball collects leaves.

cards.headline: Added along the way
cards.body: Much of the Robin you know arrived later. Maid Marian isn’t in the medieval ballads; she came from a separate shepherd-and-shepherdess love story that merged with the legend in the 16th century. Plays by Anthony Munday in 1598–99 made Robin a dispossessed earl, loyal to King Richard. A legend works like a snowball: it picks up whatever it rolls through.

cards.headline: Arthur: from battles to a king
cards.body: Arthur’s trail starts in the Historia Brittonum, compiled in Wales around 800 to 830: the earliest known mention of him. It lists 12 battles he fought against the Saxons, Level 9’s newcomers. Then Geoffrey of Monmouth’s History of the Kings of Britain (1135–38) turned him into a glorious king who defeated a Roman army. Some of Geoffrey’s story was plain invention.

cards.headline: Knights, a Grail and a round of retellings
cards.body: The French poet Chrétien de Troyes, in the late 12th century, introduced the Grail quest and the love of Lancelot and Guinevere. In the late 15th century Thomas Malory’s Le Morte Darthur passed the legend on to English readers. Every age gave Arthur what it wanted: a warrior, then a king, then a romance.

title: The Holy Roman Empire
objective: After this level you can explain what the Holy Roman Empire was, and what it was not.
summary: Often dated from Otto I's crowning in 962 to 1806, the Holy Roman Empire had elected German emperors and became a loose federation. Voltaire mocked it as neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.

cards.headline: “Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.” That was Voltaire’s verdict.
cards.body: The French writer Voltaire aimed that line at the Holy Roman Empire in 1756. Was he fair? Test the name one word at a time.

cards.headline: An emperor crowned in Rome
cards.body: The story usually starts in 962, when the German king Otto I was crowned emperor in Rome by Pope John XII. The name grew slowly: “Holy” joined it in 1157, and the full “Holy Roman Empire” was in use from 1254. It lasted until 1806, when Francis II gave up the title after Napoleon’s rise. More than eight centuries, give or take a word.

mascot.line: Two empires both calling themselves Roman. Somebody should have checked the label.

cards.headline: Roman? Remember Level 4
cards.body: Start with “Roman”. Its emperors were German kings like Otto, crowned in Rome. Meanwhile, as Level 4 showed, the Byzantines in Constantinople called themselves Romaioi, Romans, and their empire was the eastern half of the Roman Empire itself. Two empires, one Roman name. Voltaire had a point.

cards.headline: An empire? Ask the electors
cards.body: Now “empire”. The emperor wasn’t simply born to the job; he was elected. The Golden Bull of 1356 fixed the electors at seven: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, and the rulers of Bohemia, the Palatinate, Saxony and Brandenburg. By the 16th century the empire had become a loose federation. Less a single empire, more a club whose members chose their chairman.

title: Checkpoint: Kings, Parliaments and Law
objective: After this level you can explain how kings, parliaments and courts shared power by 1450.
summary: By 1450 an English king ruled alongside a charter kings kept reconfirming, a Parliament that granted taxes and courts of common law and juries. A timeline from 1166 to 1431 ties the chapter together.

cards.headline: Chapter 8 finale: by the late Middle Ages, England’s king no longer ruled alone.
cards.body: A charter kings kept reconfirming, a Parliament that held the purse strings, and courts of common law and juries. Let’s put the chapter on one page.

cards.headline: The charter that wouldn’t die
cards.body: Remember Level 71’s flop, annulled within ten weeks? Kings kept confirming it: modern research counts as many as 44 reaffirmations, the last in 1423. In 1297 it was recorded in the Statute Rolls for the first time. By the 14th century, Parliament’s regular reconfirmations were a public reminder that the king had to uphold the rule of law. The king still ruled. He just no longer ruled alone.

cards.headline: Three checks on a crown
cards.body: Put the chapter together and you get three checks. Magna Carta: no free man imprisoned without lawful judgment or the law of the land. Parliament: extra taxes for war needed its agreement. Common law: judges followed earlier decisions, so the law was common to all England, not the whim of the day.

title: The Great Famine
objective: After this level you can describe the famine that began in 1315 and its causes.
summary: From 1315, torrential rain ruined harvests across northern Europe. Animal disease, soaring prices and war turned bad weather into the worst European famine by share of population.

cards.headline: In 1315 it started raining. For the harvest, it never really stopped.
cards.body: Nobody in northern Europe had seen a summer like it. Then came another. How does rain turn into the worst famine in European history?

cards.headline: The summer that drowned the fields
cards.body: Torrential rain struck France from April 1315 and England from May, and the harvests failed. We don’t only have chroniclers’ word for it. Tree rings, nature’s weather diary, show that the growing seasons of 1314 to 1316 were the fifth wettest in Europe between 1300 and 2012. Picture your garden after a soggy week. Now picture three summers of it.

cards.fact: In England, wheat cost up to eight times as much in 1315 as in 1313.
cards.context: Wheat that sold for five shillings in 1313 fetched as much as forty by 1315. The hunger stretched from Ireland to Poland and from Scandinavia to central France. Measured by deaths as a share of the population, it was the worst famine Europe has known.

mascot.line: Bad weather empties a field. It takes a lot more to empty a whole continent’s pantry.

cards.headline: Not just the weather
cards.body: Rain started it, but the historian William Chester Jordan shows how much else piled on: diseases that killed farm animals, one failed harvest after another, wild swings in prices, and wars that got in the way of moving food. Full recovery took until 1322. A famine is rarely just about the sky. It is about everything that decides whether food reaches your table.

title: The Black Death Arrives
objective: After this level you can explain how the Black Death reached Europe in 1347.
summary: The Black Death began in Central Asia, struck the Mongol siege of Caffa in 1346, and reached Messina on ships in October 1347. By 1350 it had crossed Europe, killing an estimated 30-50% of its people.

cards.headline: October 1347: ships reach Sicily carrying a passenger nobody can see.
cards.body: Within a few years it had crossed the whole continent. Where did the Black Death come from, and how many people did it kill?

cards.headline: It began far to the east
cards.body: The trail starts in Central Asia. Near Lake Issyk-Kul, in today’s Kyrgyzstan, graves with tombstones dated 1338 and 1339 held plague DNA, pointing there as the source. By 1346 it had reached Crimea, where a Mongol army besieging the Italian trading port of Caffa began to die of it. One chronicler claimed the besiegers catapulted corpses over the walls, though he probably wasn’t there to see it. Genoese ships then carried the plague west.

title: How the Plague Spread
objective: After this level you can explain what caused the plague and how it spread.
summary: Ancient DNA from London plague-pit teeth confirmed the bacterium Yersinia pestis caused the Black Death. How it spread is still debated: rat fleas, or human fleas and lice (Dean et al. 2018).

cards.headline: What caused the Black Death? The answer was hiding in teeth.
cards.body: For centuries people could only guess. In 2011 scientists read the killer’s DNA. But one big question is still open: how did it get from person to person?

cards.headline: Case closed: Yersinia pestis
cards.body: Plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis. To test whether it was behind the Black Death, scientists went to a 14th-century plague pit at East Smithfield in London and, in 2011, sequenced the bacterium’s genome from victims’ teeth. The verdict: Yersinia pestis. It’s the medical version of finding the culprit’s fingerprints at the scene. Today, plague can be cured with antibiotics if treated quickly.

items.label: Bubonic plague
points: Usually spread by bites from infected fleas
Causes swollen, painful lymph nodes called buboes

items.label: Pneumonic plague
points: The only form that spreads person to person, through respiratory droplets

mascot.line: Science at work: a good story meets the evidence, and the evidence gets a vote.

cards.headline: Rats on trial
cards.body: The textbook story blames rats: infected fleas jump from rodents to people, which is how plague spreads today. In 2018 a team led by Katharine Dean tested that story against death records from nine European outbreaks, from 1348 to 1813. In seven of the nine, a model where human fleas and body lice passed plague between people fit the records better than rats did. Other historians disagree, and the debate is still open. The rat isn’t acquitted. It just has company.

title: A World Changed by Plague
objective: After this level you can explain how the Black Death changed wages, work and faith.
summary: With workers scarce after the Black Death, wages rose and England tried to freeze them in 1351. Fear drove flagellant processions and the false blaming and massacre of Jews, as at Strasbourg in 1349.

cards.headline: When around a third of England died, workers could name their price. Almost.
cards.body: The Black Death rewired work, pay and faith. Some of what followed was hopeful. Some was horrifying.

cards.headline: Workers become scarce, and pricey
cards.body: With so many dead, there were suddenly too few hands. The labour shortage pushed up wages for artisans and other workers, and landowners began swapping the old labour services for wages or money rents. With land cheap and pay high, many survivors lived better than before. Supply and demand, medieval edition: when workers are rare, workers cost more.

cards.headline: The lords push back
cards.body: England’s rulers tried to turn the clock back. The Statute of Labourers of 1351 tried to freeze wages at pre-plague levels and stop workers moving to find better pay. You can pass a law against arithmetic, but the arithmetic doesn’t read it.

cards.headline: Whips and repentance
cards.body: Some read the plague as God’s punishment. Groups of flagellants marched from town to town, whipping themselves to atone for their sins and calling on everyone to repent.

cards.headline: The search for someone to blame
cards.body: Fear also turned to murder. Jews were falsely accused of causing the plague by poisoning wells, and across Europe many were killed by mobs or burned. In Strasbourg, on 14 February 1349, about 2,000 Jews were burned, a city chronicler recorded. The plague only reached Strasbourg that summer. Jews were dying of the plague too, yet the accusation was widely believed. At Avignon, Pope Clement VI protected them.

title: The Peasants' Revolt
objective: After this level you can explain why English peasants rose up in 1381.
summary: Angry at wage limits since 1351 and set off by the poll tax of 1380, rebels led by Wat Tyler reached London in 1381. Tyler was killed and the promises forgotten, but no poll tax came for 250 years.

cards.headline: In June 1381, rebels marched into London to talk to their king. He was 14.
cards.body: It was one of the largest popular uprisings in medieval Europe. What made ordinary people rise, and what did they win?

cards.headline: The last straw
cards.body: Remember Level 84’s law freezing wages at pre-plague levels? Workers who knew they were scarce had resented its limits for thirty years. Then came the unpopular poll tax of 1380, and in 1381 revolt broke out. Anger that builds for a generation rarely needs much of a spark.

cards.headline: Who was then a gentleman?
cards.body: The rebels had a preacher. John Ball, a priest excommunicated for preaching a classless society, asked: “When Adam dug and Eve spun, who was then a gentleman?” In other words: in the Garden of Eden, nobody was a lord. A very short sermon, with a very long reach.

cards.headline: Promises at Mile End, a killing at Smithfield
cards.body: Led by Wat Tyler, the rebels entered London on 13 June. At Mile End, the young Richard II promised to abolish serfdom and forced labour. At a second meeting, at Smithfield, the mayor of London, William Walworth, cut Tyler down in front of the king. The revolt fell apart, and the promises were promptly forgotten.

mascot.line: Lost the battle, won a very long argument about taxes.

cards.fact: No poll tax was levied again for more than 250 years.
cards.context: The rebels lost the fight and their leader, and the king broke his word. But the tax that lit the fire did not come back for more than two and a half centuries.

title: Gunpowder Arrives
objective: After this level you can explain how gunpowder weapons changed war.
summary: Black powder, which came from China, fired European guns from the 14th century. Giant guns like Mons Meg followed, and by 1494 French cannon took castle after castle in Italy.

cards.headline: For centuries, stone walls beat armies. Then came a black powder.
cards.body: It had travelled a very long way, from China. By the end of the Middle Ages it had turned castles from fortresses into targets.

cards.headline: From fireworks to firearms
cards.body: Black powder is a mix of saltpetre, sulfur and charcoal. It is thought to have originated in China, where by the 10th century it lit fireworks and signals. Europe put it to a harsher use: from the 14th century, it fired guns. Before gunpowder, a weapon was only as strong as the muscles behind it. Now the power came from chemistry.

cards.fact: Mons Meg weighed six tonnes and fired 150 kg stones.
cards.context: She was made in the town of Mons and given to King James II of Scotland in 1457. Each gunstone weighed about as much as two grown men, and could fly up to 3.2 km. Try building a wall for that.

mascot.line: All that lovely stonework, and the new answer was simply: louder.

cards.headline: The wall stops working
cards.body: Castles were built to beat muscle, not chemistry. When French troops marched through Italy in 1494, their guns reduced castle after castle with astonishing speed. Firearms were improving so fast in the 15th and 16th centuries that military architecture had to change completely. The age of the medieval castle was over.

title: The Fall of Constantinople
objective: After this level you can explain how the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.
summary: In 1453 the 21-year-old Sultan Mehmed II broke Constantinople's walls with Urban's cannon, hauled ships overland past the harbor chain, took the city on 29 May and made it his capital.

cards.headline: Level 4’s land walls had stood since 412. In 1453 a young sultan brought cannon.
cards.body: His name was Mehmed II, and he was 21. How did he take the city nobody could take?

cards.headline: A gunsmith named Urban
cards.body: Mehmed hired a Hungarian gunsmith, Urban, to build cannon powerful enough to bring the walls down. From 6 April 1453 the guns pounded away. Between 60,000 and 80,000 Ottoman soldiers, with 69 cannon, faced only 6,000 to 7,000 trained defenders. Remember Level 4’s moat, outer wall and main wall? Cannon didn’t have to climb them. It battered a breach straight through.

mascot.line: Nobody guards the hillside against boats. That was rather the point.

cards.headline: Ships over the hill
cards.body: The city’s harbor, the Golden Horn, was sealed by a great chain. Mehmed’s answer: go around it. His men built an oiled wooden ramp and hauled smaller ships overland, and by 22 April they were inside, past the chain. If the door is locked, carry the boat around the house.

cards.headline: 29 May 1453
cards.body: The final assault came in the early hours of 29 May. The last emperor, Constantine XI, is reported to have been killed, either fighting near the breach or fleeing. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, Level 5’s great church, and converted it into a mosque. He moved his capital from Edirne to Constantinople, and the Byzantine Empire came to an end.

title: The Wars of the Roses
objective: After this level you can explain the fight between two families for England's crown.
summary: From 1455 to 1485 the houses of Lancaster and York fought for England's throne. Henry Tudor won at Bosworth, where Richard III died; Richard's skeleton turned up under a Leicester car park in 2012.

cards.headline: In 2012, archaeologists dug up a car park in Leicester and found a king.
cards.body: He had died in battle in 1485, at the end of a thirty-year family feud over England’s crown. How did that feud start, and how did it end?

cards.headline: Two houses, one crown
cards.body: From 1455 to 1485, two branches of one royal family, the houses of Lancaster and York, fought for the throne. Both were descended from Edward III. The trouble began at the top: King Henry VI suffered spells of madness, and powerful nobles with private armies ran riot. The first battle came at St Albans in 1455. A family inheritance fight, with armies instead of lawyers.

cards.headline: Roses, added later
cards.body: Nobody at the time called them the Wars of the Roses. The name came long afterward, from the supposed badges of the two sides: the white rose of York and the red rose of Lancaster. A lovely name for a very bloody business.

cards.headline: Bosworth, and a wedding
cards.body: On 22 August 1485 Henry Tudor defeated Richard III at Bosworth Field, and Richard was killed. As Henry VII, he married Elizabeth of York in 1486, joining the rival claims in one marriage and founding the Tudor dynasty. The feud that started with a battle ended with a wedding.

mascot.line: Next time you can’t find a parking space, remember: one was taken by a king.

cards.headline: The king in the car park
cards.body: Richard’s grave was lost for centuries. In September 2012 a University of Leicester team dug where the Grey Friars church once stood, now a car park, and found a skeleton with a curved spine and battle wounds. DNA matched living relatives of his family line, and in 2013 the university announced it was Richard III beyond reasonable doubt.

title: The Rise of the Ottomans
objective: After this level you can describe how the Ottoman Empire grew.
summary: Founded by Osman I about 1300, the Ottomans crossed into Europe as Byzantine allies and took Gallipoli in 1354. Nearly destroyed by Timur in 1402, they reunited by 1413 and lasted until 1922.

cards.headline: Around 1300, the Ottomans were a small band in Anatolia. They lasted 600+ years.
cards.body: Level 87 showed them taking Constantinople. How did a chief’s followers get that far, and why did they nearly not make it?

cards.headline: Osman’s people, invited in
cards.body: The name comes from the founder: Osman I, a Turkmen chief who founded the dynasty and the empire about 1300, near Bursa in Anatolia. His son Orhan’s big break came from the Byzantines themselves. He crossed into the Balkans as the ally of a future emperor, John VI, and married his daughter Theodora. In 1354 the Ottomans took Gallipoli as a permanent foothold in Europe. Some guests never leave.

cards.headline: An army that never went home
cards.body: From the late 14th century the sultans built an elite corps, the Janissaries. They were recruited by taking Christian boys from the Balkans and converting them to Islam. They are called the first modern standing army in Europe: soldiers kept permanently ready, not called up for one campaign.

cards.headline: Nearly the end, in 1402
cards.body: Then a bigger conqueror arrived. In 1402 Timur, from Central Asia, crushed Sultan Bayezid I near Ankara, and Bayezid died in captivity. Timur split the Ottoman lands among Bayezid’s sons, who fought each other until Mehmed I reunited them in 1413. Forty years later, Mehmed II took Constantinople. Knocked down, not knocked out.

cards.context: At its height it reached the gates of Vienna. From a frontier band around 1300, it lasted more than 600 years, long after the Middle Ages had ended.

title: The Printing Press
objective: After this level you can explain how Gutenberg's press changed Europe after 1450.
summary: Around 1450 in Mainz, Gutenberg printed with reusable metal type. By 1500 Europe's few thousand manuscript books had become more than 9 million printed ones.

cards.headline: Before printing, Europe’s books numbered in the thousands. By 1500: millions.
cards.body: Remember Level 7’s monks, copying every book letter by letter? One workshop in Mainz changed the arithmetic. How?

cards.headline: Letters you can use again
cards.body: Johannes Gutenberg worked on his invention in Strasbourg and Mainz, and by about 1450 it was working well. The secret was movable type: single letters cast from a metal alloy that melted easily and cooled quickly into tough, reusable pieces. Set them in lines, print a page, then break them up and set the next. A scribe wrote every letter of every copy. Gutenberg’s letters worked like Scrabble tiles you could play again and again.

cards.headline: Borrowed from the wine press
cards.body: To press ink onto a page firmly and evenly, Gutenberg built a press, probably adapted from the ones used for wine, oil or paper. His showpiece, the 42-line Bible, came off it in Mainz around 1455, in a run of perhaps as many as 180 copies. About a quarter were printed on vellum, the same animal skin the monks of Level 7 wrote on. Old material, new machine.

mascot.line: Fifty years from a few thousand books to millions. That’s what happens when copying stops being handwork.

cards.headline: From thousands to millions
cards.body: Before printing, Europe’s manuscript books could be counted in thousands. By 1500, after only 50 years of printing, there were more than 9 million. Why so fast? A printer ran off a whole edition at once, usually about 250 copies, and the Venetian printer Aldus Manutius printed 1,000. Remember that a monastery with 600 books had a large library? One print run could now outnumber it.
