title: The Renaissance Begins
objective: After this level you can explain how Italian cities led a revival of ancient learning.
summary: The Renaissance, or rebirth, began in 14th-century Italy. Rich cities like Florence paid for it, and humanists like Poggio hunted ancient texts in medieval monastery libraries.

cards.headline: In 1417 an Italian book hunter went searching monasteries for ancient Rome.
cards.body: He came home with a lost Roman poem. His name was Poggio Bracciolini, and he wasn’t the only one hunting. Why were Italians suddenly so hungry for old books?

cards.headline: A rebirth
cards.body: Renaissance is French for “rebirth”. It began in Italy in the 14th century, with a surge of interest in the learning of ancient Greece and Rome. Remember Level 2’s Petrarch, who saw ancient Rome as the light? His followers, the humanists, set out to bring that light back. Calling the centuries in between the “Middle Ages” was their way of saying: we’re the sequel.

cards.headline: Florence pays the bills
cards.body: Why Italy? Its city-states were rich from trade, and their wealthy families spent on culture. In Florence the greatest of them, the Medici, paid to build and decorate palaces, churches and monasteries. Money bought beauty, and a great deal of it.

mascot.line: The people who called the Middle Ages dark were reading by its light.

cards.headline: Rescued by the monks
cards.body: Here’s the twist. Where did Poggio find his lost classics? In medieval monasteries: two unknown speeches by Cicero at Cluny, and at St. Gall the first complete text of Quintilian’s handbook on public speaking. The Renaissance called the Middle Ages dark, then built itself from books the monks had copied (Level 7). The rebirth was delivered by medieval midwives.

cards.headline: Poggio’s handwriting, your typeface
cards.body: Poggio also copied books himself, and he developed a new handwriting: round and formal, based on an older medieval script. After a generation of polishing by scribes, it became the model for roman type, the upright letters early printers set in metal. The Renaissance’s look began as one book hunter’s pen.

title: Ships and Navigation

summary: Portugal's caravels, with triangular sails that could beat against the wind, carried explorers down Africa's coast: to the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 and India in 1498.

cards.headline: “Henry the Navigator” never went on a voyage of exploration.
cards.body: Portugal’s Prince Henry paid for them instead. His captains needed a ship that could probe an unknown coast and still get home. What did they build?

cards.headline: A ship that sails into the wind
cards.body: The Portuguese developed the caravel to explore Africa’s coast: a light ship with two or three masts and triangular lateen sails. Its great advantage was that it could sail against the wind, zig-zagging forward. On a coast where the wind kept blowing the wrong way, that was the difference between exploring and being stuck. Out of sight of land, sailors trusted a compass, known to European mariners since the 12th century.

cards.headline: Gold, and people
cards.body: Why keep sailing south? Henry wanted a share of West Africa’s trade, especially in gold and in enslaved people. In 1441 a caravel came home with both, and the costly voyages suddenly paid. It’s an uncomfortable fact worth keeping: from the start, these voyages traded in human beings.

title: Columbus in 1492
objective: After this level you can explain Columbus's voyage and why 1492 is a turning point.
summary: Columbus sailed west in 1492 thinking Earth was smaller than it is, and reached the Bahamas believing it was Asia. For the Taino he met, it began enslavement, disease and collapse.

cards.headline: Columbus didn’t set out to prove the Earth was round. Everyone educated knew.
cards.body: So what did he actually get wrong? And what did his landing in 1492 set in motion for the people who were already there?

cards.headline: Three ships west
cards.body: Funded by Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos on August 3, 1492, with three ships. Two of them, the Niña and the Pinta, were caravels, the ships of Level 93. On October 12 he reached the Bahamas, and he believed he had arrived in Asia.

cards.headline: Round, but smaller
cards.body: Educated Europeans had known Earth was a sphere since at least the early 7th century. Columbus’s mistake was size: he believed Earth was much smaller than it is, and Asia much farther east. The flat-Earth version of his story was popularized by Washington Irving’s 1828 biography, which filled gaps with invented details. The real Columbus wasn’t a brave rebel against flat-Earthers. He was a confident man with the wrong numbers.

mascot.line: A turning point isn’t always a triumph. For the Taíno, 1492 was the start of a catastrophe.

cards.headline: What 1492 cost
cards.body: The people Columbus met were the Taíno, the most numerous people of the Caribbean, perhaps one or two million strong. Columbus decided they would make ideal slaves. In 1495 his forces killed and captured many on Hispaniola, and he shipped 500 to Spain; some 200 died on the way. Those left behind were forced to pay tribute in gold or cotton. Enslavement, violence, starvation and diseases brought by the Spanish followed. By 1520 the Taíno were reduced to a few thousand.
cards.callout: The Taíno: perhaps 1 to 2 million at contact; a few thousand by 1520

cards.headline: Why 1492 is a turning point
cards.body: Older accounts crowned Columbus the “discoverer” of a New World, though Native Americans had lived there long before him. Historians now focus on what his voyages unleashed: the slave trade and the ravages of imported disease. That’s why 1492 matters so much. It joined two worlds, at a terrible price.

title: Mali and Mansa Musa
objective: After this level you can describe the empire of Mali and Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage.
summary: Mali grew rich on gold and salt. On his 1324 hajj, Mansa Musa gave away so much gold that its value fell in Cairo; 'richest person ever' is a popular claim nobody can measure.

cards.headline: In 1375 a mapmaker in Majorca drew an African king holding a ball of gold.
cards.body: The king was Mansa Musa of Mali, and the map called him the richest and noblest king of his land. Why did a European map need him in it?

cards.headline: An empire built on gold
cards.body: Mali began as a small kingdom on the upper Niger River. In the 1230s its founder, Sundiata, built it into an empire, and his armies secured gold-bearing lands to the south. Mali grew rich by controlling the trade in gold and salt. Under Mansa Musa (mansa means emperor) it took in the trading cities of Timbuktu and Gao. Musa said it took a year to cross his empire.

cards.headline: The hajj of 1324
cards.body: In 1324 Musa made the hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, and passed through Cairo with a huge caravan. The Arab historian al-Umari, who came to Egypt a few years later, wrote down what Cairo remembered: Musa left no court official without the gift of a load of gold. So much gold was spent that its value fell, and it still hadn’t recovered about twelve years later. Imagine a visitor so generous he lowered the price of gold.

mascot.line: When a number sounds too good to check, ask who could possibly have counted it.

cards.headline: The richest person ever?
cards.body: You’ll often read that Mansa Musa was the richest person in history. It’s a popular claim, and an old one: remember that map. But historians say his wealth is impossible to calculate accurately. Comparing a 14th-century emperor’s gold with a modern fortune is guesswork. Fabulously rich? Certainly. Richest ever? Nobody can know.

cards.headline: Gold into learning
cards.body: Back from Mecca, Musa had a great mosque, the Djinguereber, built in Timbuktu, and the city grew into a center of Islamic scholarship. The gold that dazzled Cairo also paid for books and teachers at home.

title: Great Zimbabwe
objective: After this level you can describe the stone city of Great Zimbabwe and its trade.
summary: Ancestors of the Shona built Great Zimbabwe's mortarless stone walls and grew rich on gold trade with the Indian Ocean coast; colonial-era claims of foreign builders were false.

cards.headline: A whole country is named after a medieval city of stone.
cards.body: Zimbabwe takes its name from a Shona word meaning “stone houses”. The ruins that inspired it were once the heart of a kingdom. Who built them? For decades, some people refused to accept the answer.

cards.headline: Walls without mortar
cards.body: Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona people and flourished between the 11th and 15th centuries, home at its height to 10,000 to 20,000 people. Its Great Enclosure is the largest ancient structure in sub-Saharan Africa. The granite walls stand about 10 metres high in places, laid in careful layers without mortar. Nothing holds them up but skill and gravity.

cards.headline: Gold for the world
cards.body: The city grew rich on cattle, crops and trade in gold with the coast of the Indian Ocean. Archaeologists digging there have found goods from far away: Syrian glass, Chinese celadon dishes and Persian bowls. Chinese dishes on a Shona table: that’s how far the gold reached.

cards.headline: The wrong answers
cards.body: Late 19th-century Europeans refused to credit Africans. One linked the ruins to the Queen of Sheba, another to Phoenicians or Arabians. None of it was true. In 1905 the archaeologist David Randall-MacIver showed the ruins were medieval and entirely African, and Gertrude Caton-Thompson confirmed it in 1929. Even so, from 1965 to 1980 Rhodesia’s ruling party censored what could be published about the site. The evidence never changed. The politics did.

title: The Americas Before 1492
objective: After this level you can describe the Maya, Aztec and Inca before Europeans arrived.
summary: Before 1492 the Americas held the Maya and their writing, the Aztec island capital Tenochtitlan, the Inca empire of the Andes and Cahokia, the largest city north of Mexico.

cards.headline: In 1492 the Americas weren’t a new world. They were full of old ones.
cards.body: Cities, empires and writing had flourished there for centuries. Four stops before Columbus arrived: the Maya, the Aztecs, the Inca and Cahokia.

cards.headline: The Maya: writing in stone
cards.body: Maya cities flourished in their Classic period, about 250 to 900. The Maya developed the only true writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas. The great lowland cities were abandoned around 900, but the Maya didn’t vanish: millions speak Mayan languages today.

cards.headline: The Aztecs: a city on a lake
cards.body: The Mexica, better known as the Aztecs, founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco, linked to the shore by causeways. How many lived there by 1519? Estimates run from about 50,000 to 400,000. Why such a gap? No reliable census survives, so scholars estimate from the city’s area and how densely people probably lived.

cards.headline: The Inca: roads and knots
cards.body: The Inca ruled along the Andes and the Pacific coast, from northern Ecuador to central Chile. Two great roads ran north to south, each about 3,600 km long, and relay runners carried messages as quipu, knotted cords. In 1532 the empire probably held about 12 million people, though estimates vary.

mascot.line: Notice the ranges. Honest history says “about” and “estimates vary” when nobody took a census.

cards.headline: Cahokia: a city on the Mississippi
cards.body: North of Mexico, the largest city was Cahokia, near modern St. Louis, which flourished from about 950 to 1350. Its Monks Mound rises 30 meters, the largest prehistoric earthen structure in the Western Hemisphere. Estimates of its peak population run from 8,000 to 40,000.

title: When Did the Middle Ages End?
objective: After this level you can compare the dates historians use for the end of the Middle Ages.
summary: Historians end the Middle Ages at different dates, most often 1453, 1492 or 1517. Each marks a different kind of change, and all sit near the round figure of about 1500.

cards.headline: The Middle Ages have a neat start. The finish line is a matter of opinion.
cards.body: Remember Level 1’s sunrise: easy to see it has happened, hard to name the minute. Historians still pick different minutes. Here are the favorites.

events.label: Gutenberg’s press is working in Mainz
The Ottomans take Constantinople
Columbus sails west to the Americas
Luther’s Ninety-five Theses begin the Reformation

cards.headline: 1453: Rome’s other half falls
cards.body: The oldest favorite is 1453, when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II took Constantinople and ended the Byzantine Empire. It makes neat bookends: the Middle Ages begin when Rome falls in the West in 476, and end when the Roman East falls too, about a thousand years later.

cards.headline: 1492 and 1517
cards.body: Others choose 1492, when Columbus’s voyage joined Europe to the Americas. Others pick 1517, when Martin Luther’s Ninety-five Theses began the Reformation, which reshaped Western Christianity. Luther’s ideas were printed and reprinted within weeks and read across Europe. The new age spread on the last one’s best invention.

mascot.line: Pick 1453, 1492 or 1517 and you’re in good company. Just say which, and why.

cards.headline: So which is right?
cards.body: Each date answers a different question: power (1453), the wider world (1492), faith (1517). That’s why the round figure you met in Level 1 is “about 1500”: all three candidates sit close to it. The Middle Ages didn’t end on a day. They faded, like that sunrise, only in reverse.

title: What the Middle Ages Left Us
objective: After this level you can name medieval inventions and institutions we still use.
summary: Eyeglasses, mechanical clocks, roman type and civil law all come down to us from the Middle Ages.

cards.headline: If you wear glasses, you’re wearing a medieval invention.
cards.body: The Middle Ages ended, but they never quite left. Some of what they made is on your face, on your wall and in the law.

cards.headline: A friar remembers
cards.body: Eyeglasses were first made in Italy, most probably in Pisa, around 1290; the first ones helped farsighted people read. How do we know the date? In a sermon of 1306, the friar Giordano da Pisa said the art of making them was not yet twenty years old, and that he had talked to the man who discovered it. The inventor’s name is lost. The invention is not.

cards.headline: Clocks that rang
cards.body: The first mechanical clocks we clearly know of were large, weight-driven machines in towers. They struck the hours rather than showing them, which is why the word clock comes from medieval Latin clocca, “bell”. England’s oldest surviving one, at Salisbury Cathedral, dates from 1386. Every alarm on your phone has a bell in its family tree.

mascot.line: Glasses, clocks, letters, laws. Not bad for an age once called dark.

cards.headline: Law and letters
cards.body: Some legacies you can’t see. Justinian’s code (Level 5) became the foundation of civil law, used today across continental Europe and Latin America. And roman type, the upright letters of printed books, began as Poggio’s humanist handwriting (Level 92). You read and live by medieval inventions every day.
